system_prompt:
Reasoning: medium
You are a research assistant. Your only tool is `web_search` (up to 10 searches).
After each search, the most promising results are opened automatically, their links
are followed, and notes from the most relevant pages come back with the results.
Your job is to write the queries that reach the right pages.

Each query targets one page that would state or link to a missing fact: an entity's
profile, a discography or list, an official record, an interview, an article.
Do not put the whole question into one query.
- Use enough words to preserve the identifying relation. Combine two or three
  distinctive conditions when helpful; there is no fixed word-count limit.
  Quote exact names or titles, not generic descriptions.
- Distinguish question-given constraints, source-supported facts and guesses.
  Do not turn a guessed country, nationality, date or identity into a required
  query filter. Search the stated relation before assuming its answer values.
  If a hypothesis-specific query finds no support, remove that assumed filter
  and return to the question's constraints rather than cycling through guesses.
- Once a candidate appears, search the candidate's name with the condition still
  unverified (e.g. `<name> interview 2013`, `<name> discography label`).
- Reuse exact names, titles and terms from the notes; they are better query words
  than paraphrases of the question.
- Review candidates in the returned notes before every search. Keep new candidates
  pending until investigated or explicitly excluded by source evidence. Prefer
  checking a distinctive missing condition of a source-backed candidate before
  returning to an unsupported guess. If you defer a candidate, explain why.
- Never repeat or lightly reword an earlier query. If a query returned nothing
  useful, switch to a different clue or a different kind of source, not a synonym.

Before each search, write in your reasoning: the current candidate(s), which
conditions are confirmed, contradicted or unknown, and what the next query should
find.

Notes are free-form readings of individual pages. Treat reported source facts
as evidence and tentative candidates as leads to verify. A mention alone does
not establish all conditions. Compare candidates against every
condition, revise on explicit contradictions, and preserve unknowns as unknowns.
When evidence supports an answer, give it in the requested format with source URLs.
Never invent missing facts or treat a JEV ranking score as answer confidence.

# 2001 Contest Winners

Staff November 9, 2010

## Florida Press Club Excellence In Journalism Contest 2001 Winners

(If your name is misspelled, please message Jennifer Cason at [contest@floridapressclub.org](mailto:contest@floridapressclub.org).)

## Frances DeVore Award for Public Service

**Class A:**

First Place – Staff, Orlando Sentinel

Second Place – Fred Schulte and Jenni Bergal, South Florida Sun-Sentinel

Third Place – Ronnie Greene and Geoff Doughter, Miami Herald

**Classes B:**

First Place – Brigid O’Malley, Naples Daily News

Second Place – Todd Twilley, News-Herald

Third Place – Jeff Lytle, Naples Daily News

**Classes C-D:**

First Place – Peter B. Gallagher and Charles Flowers, The Seminole Tribune

## President’s Special Award for Election Coverage

**Class A-B:**

First Place – The Palm Beach Post

Second Place – The Orlando Sentinel

Third Place – The Tallahassee Democrat

**Classes C-D:**

First Place – Staff, Palm Beach Daily News

# EWA Awards

[Awards Rules](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#AwardsRules)

[FAQs](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#FAQs)

[Special Awards](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#SpecialAwards)

## EWA's National Awards for Education Reporting

The National Awards for Education Reporting advance education journalism by recognizing the field’s very best efforts. Organized by the Education Writers Association, the awards’ goals are to:

*   Encourage and inspire more and better education journalism;
*   Underscore the importance of excellent coverage and storytelling as a cornerstone of education and democracy.

All full-time and freelance reporters may participate in the awards. So whether your work appeared in print or online, on TV or the radio, or all of the above, we’re eager to recognize excellence on the education beat. We have made some changes to the awards, so please check those out.

### **Awards: Quick Facts & Rules**

*   **Early Bird Discount:** $75 for members and $125 for nonmembers to enter the awards until Dec. 19, 2025 at 2 p.m. Eastern.
*   **Regular Price:** $125 for members and $175 for nonmembers to enter the awards until Jan. 7, 2026 at 6 p.m. Eastern. All qualified **student journalists** pay $25.[EWA membership is free.](link_50)
*   **Membership Deadlines:** Apply for membership by **Dec. 4** to be eligible for the Early Bird Discount, or [become a member](link_50) by **Dec. 15** to be eligible for the Regular Price membership discount.
*   First, [read our rules](link_51) and **FAQs** below. Next, [create an account, and submit your entry here](link_52).

[View Awards Rules](link_51)

**Have any questions? Email [awards@ewa.org](mailto:awards@ewa.org)**

 2025 EWA Awards 

## FAQs

 01 

[Entry Fees & Refunds](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 02 

[How Do I Enter?](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 03 

[Who Can Enter?](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 04 

[Which Category Is Best?](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 05 

[Supplemental Materials](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 06 

[Newsroom Size Division](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 07 

[Rules & Criteria](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 08 

[Cash Prizes & Judging](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards#)

 01 

#### **What is the latest date for entering?**

All entries must be completed before **6 p.m. Eastern** on **Jan. 7, 2026.**

**_Please note:_**Entries submitted by**2 p.m. Eastern**on**Dec. 19, 2025**are charged **$75 for members**and**$125**for nonmembers.**Fees increase to $125 for members**and**$175 for non-members**after **2 p.m. Dec. 19, 2025**until the **Jan. 7, 2026 deadline.**Student journalists pay $25.

**_EWA Membership Deadlines:_**Become a member by **Dec. 4**to receive the Early Bird Discount. Become a member by **Dec. 15** to pay the Regular Price discount.

**Are the fees per article or per entry?**The payment is per entry, not per article. For example, if a category permits up to three articles or pieces, and you submit three articles for that entry, you pay a $75 early bird fee for members or $125 early bird fee for nonmembers.

**May I send my payment for entry later?**********No. We only accept credit card payments. If there are extenuating circumstances, email [awards@ewa.org](mailto:awards@ewa.org) to make a request.

**May I take back an entry I submitted? What about a refund?**

Once an entry is submitted, you cannot delete it, nor can we refund your application fee.

**I joined EWA one day before the deadline, and I haven’t heard back. What happens?**

To receive the member discount, entrants must adhere to EWA’s deadlines for membership. The membership deadlines are listed above in this section.

If you’re a nonmember thinking about entering the EWA Awards and want to save money, we highly recommend joining EWA sooner rather than later. At times, it takes a week for our membership coordinator to review your application, so applying with enough time for this process is important.

 02 

**What is the latest date for entering?**

All entries must be completed before **6 p.m. Eastern** on **Jan. 7, 2026.**

**Is there a limit to the number of entries I may submit?**

No, but each entry requires its own entry fee and entry form. Also remember, no story can be submitted in more than one category, with the exception of beat reporting.

**What if I want to submit something from a previous employer?**

If you’re entering work from a previous employer, please be sure to note that in your entry letter. You can enter it in the category size for your former employer – unless you are submitting an entry for beat reporting, and it includes stories from both your former employer and your current one. Then the category size entered must match the larger news organization.

**Can a media outlet representative submit entries on behalf of other staff members?**

Yes. Also, if you’re an editor submitting on behalf of a reporter or freelancer, please consult with them to make sure they also have not submitted the same entry. Ditto for reporters and freelancers: Please consult with your editors to make sure they have not submitted on your behalf.

 03 

**May freelance journalists enter?**

Yes, as long as they meet EWA’s definition of “journalist,” as defined in [EWA Bylaws, Article II, Section 1.1.](link_53)

Eligible journalists are defined as: “individuals whose primary professional activities involve reporting, writing, producing, editing, or otherwise preparing the news and editorial content of independent news media products. The definition of journalist also includes freelancers whose primary body of work is for independent news media, staffers at press associations or journalism education associations, journalism instructors, and journalism students.”

In categories with newsroom size subcategories, freelancers must enter according to the newsroom size of the organization that published their story. Please verify the size of the newsroom with the organization.

If you’re a freelance journalist with an LLC, you still enter according to the FTE of the**_news organization in which your submissions appeared._**

**I’m not a journalist, but I also contribute to a news outlet or magazine. May I enter?**

No. EWA only accepts entries produced by journalists that appeared in an independent journalism outlet. The majority of an entrant’s work must follow the [EWA bylaws](link_53).

**Why aren’t works by non-journalists eligible for these awards?**

There are many thoughtful writers in teaching, think tanks, and research communities who contribute to education journalism by providing news tips, quotes, research and perspectives. However, this contest honors the very best of independent education journalism. EWA is grateful to its community members for their continued support for expanding the breadth and depth of independent education journalism.

**I work for a magazine/weekly/podcast/online-only news outlet. Where should I enter?**

Journalists of any medium or platform can enter and compete in any of the categories, except those specifying a broadcast-type category. In addition, any news outlet can submit entries that are primarily audio or primarily visual.

**Do I need to be a full-time education reporter?**

No. Entries must be about education, but the journalists producing the submitted work don’t need to be assigned to the beat. You do need to qualify as a journalist as defined by EWA’s bylaws. Please see our [bylaws](link_53) for more.

 04 

**May I enter the same story in two different categories to hedge my bets?**

No. The only exception is those entered in the beat category.

**How many articles, or how much audio or video, can I submit in each entry?**

It depends on the category. All audio and video submitted to the broadcast features and news subcategories are capped at a total viewing or listening time of 15 minutes. Podcasts can have up to one hour of audio. Beat reporters can submit up to five pieces. (See [Categories](link_54) for more details.)

**I’m a radio reporter. Can I only enter broadcast news, broadcast features or podcast?**

No. Journalists at radio outlets can enter other categories, especially if they have packages that include multimedia or print.

The broadcast category is reserved for television and radio news organizations. Audio and visual news content that is published by non-broadcast (television and radio) news organizations is eligible to be entered in all other EWA Awards categories (feature, explanatory, investigative, data reporting & visualization, and beat).

**I’m a television reporter. Can I only enter broadcast (news or features)?**

No. Journalists at television outlets can enter other categories, especially if they have packages that include multimedia or print.

The broadcast category is reserved for television and radio news organizations. Audio and visual news content that is published by non-broadcast (television and radio) news organizations is eligible to be entered in all other EWA Awards categories (feature, explanatory, investigative, beat).

**I work for a small education-only outlet. Can I submit stories to the small newsroom category instead of education-only?**

No. If there is an education-only subcategory, you must choose that one. Education-only entries that were co-published with a non education-only outlet can be submitted to another subcategory if the partner outlet contributed substantially to the entry.

**I’m a student journalist. What can I enter?**

We have created a special category for student journalists. The stories should have been published or produced by a student-run independent news organization or school-related news organization in which students serve as staffers. (This can’t be an NPR affiliate linked to a university like WAMU or WUIS.) You can submit up to three stories, but they must center around a common theme.

**What’s the difference between the feature, explanatory and investigative categories?**

The explanatory category focuses on explaining complex issues or current events in education. Stories in the feature category focus on human interest or building a narrative. Investigative reporting uncovers a problem or wrong-doing and leads to change in policies.

**What happened to the news category for FTE-based newsrooms and education-only outlets?**

The majority of entries submitted to the news categories for small and large newsrooms and education-only outlets were explanatory in nature, so EWA decided to sharpen the category’s focus. Breaking news stories can still be submitted in the beat and broadcast categories.

**How do I figure out how many stories to submit?**

Whether someone scores lower in an entry often comes down to the quality of every individual piece, according to judges’ comments on multi-story entries and during their virtual final decision meetings. Entry quality can make the difference in placing fourth or as a finalist, or placing as a finalist or winner if one article is substantially weaker than the others. If a piece isn’t as strong as the others, don’t enter it. Quantity does not edge quality.

**I don’t know the newsroom’s FTE count. Does it matter?**

Yes. If you enter one of the FTE subcategories in beat reporting, explanatory journalism, feature, and investigative reporting, it is mandatory to enter a newsroom FTE count. Check with an editor or human resources at your news organization. If you’re a freelancer, do the same.

 05 

**Do I need a letter of support or endorsement from an editor?**

No. You can enter individually. You don’t need a letter or any other approval from an editor. The same rule applies for freelancers. But do submit a cover letter.

**What should I include in my cover letter?**

The cover letter can be written by the entrant(s) or an editor. Briefly state why the entry matters and include background information, if appropriate, about reporting challenges, such as whether the entry required significant public records requests, the thinking behind any innovations in presentation, and the impact of the work, such as whether it uncovered a critical issue or violation or resulted in any positive changes in the community. Judges advise against recapping your coverage. They will listen to/read/watch/your stories. The length for your cover letter is one page.

 06 

**How do I calculate the size of my newsroom to determine which division to enter?**

Calculate the journalism staff size by counting all the full-time-equivalent (FTE) journalism-related employees in the newsroom at the time the entry was produced. In addition to reporters, the calculation should include all editors, designers, online producers, and multimedia content producers, such as photographers, data analysts and videographers. Two half-time editors, for example, would add up to one FTE. If an organization has ongoing contracts with freelancers, they must be incorporated into the FTE count.

Freelancers should submit entries based on the FTE count of the media outlet that published them, not based on their LLC. Four of the awards categories include subcategories by newsroom size. _If you enter a newsroom size subcategory, include your newsroom’s FTE count on your entry._

Newsrooms sizes are:

Small: 40 and under FTE newsroom employees or under 50 broadcast market.

Large: Over 40 FTE newsroom employees or top 50 broadcast market.

**I work for a small bureau or division that is part of a large news organization. Which newsroom size do I enter?**

Enter the size division reflecting the newsroom resources available to you to produce the work. If you received no material support from any other office or division, enter based on your local newsroom. But if your work benefited from reporting from other bureaus, or editing, programming, or graphics from a centralized desk, enter in the division that corresponds to the staffing of the combined newsrooms.

**How will you know the size of my newsroom?**

We generally operate on the honor system; though if the judges check and discover you have entered a newsroom size division smaller than you should, they will disqualify your entry. If you enter a larger division than you should, they may move your submission to its rightful place. We adopted the FTE newsroom staff model of gauging the size of the publication because we believe that metric has more to do with the resources of an outlet than does circulation size or web traffic.

**I have a submission that ran as part of a partnership with another journalism organization. Which newsroom size division should I enter?**

Enter the newsroom size of the larger partner.

 07 

**What publish date should my stories have?**

Entries must have been published, posted or broadcast in an independent news outlet for the first time in 2025. EWA does accept series in which one part appeared during the 2024-25 school year, but a majority of the series’ pieces must have run in 2025. The only exception: Stories published or broadcast in 2024 that were honored as finalists or winners in last year’s contest are ineligible for consideration in this year’s awards.

**Do you accept entries in languages other than English?**

If you submit an entry in another language, you must provide an English translation or English captions/subtitles in the case of broadcast stories.

**What format should I use to submit my work?**

URLs alone are enough and preferred (though make sure to provide usernames and passwords to get around paywalls), but you can also submit JPEGs, MOVs, MPEGs, MP3s or MP4s, PDFs, PNGs, WAVs, or WMVs – we recommend you use a password-protected website like Vimeo; some judges have experienced difficulty viewing uploads. Please note that judges can disqualify submissions if they’re hard to read or view, so if you choose to submit a PDF or raw video/audio, ensure it’s readable, viewable or listenable.

**Does my entry have to be submitted online?**

Yes.

**My newsroom worked with others, and we’re submitting entries from a package in two separate categories. Is that okay?**

That is acceptable IF:

*   The stories or work are not duplicated in any category other than beat.
*   You use a separate title for each entry.
*   They match the category you are entering. If you enter a feature, it must be a feature story.

**My newsroom produced an ongoing project or series with multiple stories. May I submit individual pieces of that larger project as separate entries?**

Yes. Be sure to give each entry a distinct, unique title, so there is no confusion and to clearly differentiate it from other stories in the larger project.

**May I submit both an audio and print version of a story in two different categories?**

If the two versions are largely similar, you should only submit one of these versions as an EWA Awards entry.

 08 

**Are there cash prizes?**

First-prize winners receive $750 and a plaque. The winner of the Ronald D. Moskowitz Prize for Outstanding Beat Reporting receives $2,500, and the winner of the Fred M. Hechinger Grand Prize for Distinguished Education Reporting receives $5,000.

**When will the winners be announced?**

Finalists will be announced in late spring 2026. Winners are announced at EWA’s 2026 National Seminar in Baltimore, **June 2-5**.

**Who judges these entries?**

EWA recruits veteran reporters, editors and journalism professors, many of them previous EWA prize winners, as judges. Judges are assigned categories and newsroom divisions that avoid conflicts of interest, and they recuse themselves from judging entries from their own employer or close friends. If you would like to be considered as a judge, which is a great opportunity to read and learn about the best education journalism of the year, please email [awards@ewa.org](mailto:awards@ewa.org).

#### June 30, 2004

# 2003 Mark of Excellence Regional Award Winners

The Society of Professional Journalists congratulates the 2003 Mark of Excellence regional award winners. All winners were recognized at regional conferences nationwide throughout March, April and May. SPJ received more than 3,200 entries from undergraduate students for this year’s contest.

The Society of Professional Journalists works to improve and protect journalism. SPJ is dedicated to encouraging the free practice of journalism and stimulating high standards of ethical behavior. Founded in 1909 as Sigma Delta Chi, and based in Indianapolis, SPJ promotes the free flow of information vital to a well-informed public, works to inspire and educate the next generation of journalists, and protects First Amendment guarantees of freedom of speech and press.

# SPJ Awards

#### Awards: Important Dates

*   [2/15/27: Entry Deadline: 2026 Stillwater Awards](link_34)

###### Jump to:

— [National Contests](https://www.spj.org/awards/#1)  
— [Awards, Fellowships and Internships](https://www.spj.org/awards/#2)  
— SPJ Honors: [Public](https://www.spj.org/awards/#3) | [Members](https://www.spj.org/awards/#3b)  
— [National Chapter Awards](https://www.spj.org/awards/#4)  
— [National Contests (discontinued)](https://www.spj.org/awards/#6)  
— [Local/Regional Contests](https://www.spj.org/awards/#5)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)National SPJ Contests

#### [Sigma Delta Chi Awards](link_35)

The [Sigma Delta Chi Awards](link_35) — among the premiere prizes given in the profession — recognize achievement in professional journalism in its many forms.

[Order a duplicate plaque/certificate](link_36)

* * *

#### [Mark of Excellence Awards](link_37)

The [Mark of Excellence Awards](link_37) honor the best in collegiate journalism, judged at the regional and national levels.

[Order a duplicate plaque/certificate](link_36)

* * *

#### [SPJ National High School Essay Contest](link_38)

[SPJ wants to increase high school students’ knowledge and understanding of the importance of the Free Media to our lives](link_38). The top three national winners receive scholarship awards.

* * *

#### [New America Award](link_39)

SPJ’s [New America Award](link_39) honors public service journalism that explores and exposes issues of importance to immigrant and/or ethnic communities in the United States. [**Nominations now open.**](link_40)

[[Top]](https://www.spj.org/awards/#)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)National Awards, Fellowships and Internships

##### [Eugene S. Pulliam First Amendment Award](link_41)

Established by the Sigma Delta Chi Foundation, the Eugene S. Pulliam First Amendment Award recognizes, with a $10,000 award, accomplishments on behalf of First Amendment freedoms by an individual, group of individuals or an organization.

* * *

##### [Eugene C. Pulliam Fellowship for Public Service Journalism](link_42)

The Eugene C. Pulliam Fellowship is intended to enable a mid-career journalist who specializes in fact-based commentary or analysis to have time away from daily responsibilities to pursue in-depth reporting projects.

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)National SPJ Honors (Public)

[Distinguished Teaching in Journalism Award](link_43)  
The Award honors an outstanding journalism educator who has made a significant contribution to the profession and/or journalism education and to maintaining the highest standards of the profession.

[Ethics in Journalism Award](link_44)  
The Ethics in Journalism Award honors journalists or news organizations that perform in an outstanding ethical manner demonstrating the ideals of the SPJ Code of Ethics. It also honors especially notable efforts to educate the public on principles embodied in the code or hold journalists ethically accountable for their behavior. Nominations are open. Self-nomination is permitted.

[Fellow of the Society Award](link_45)  
The Fellows of the Society honor is presented to journalists for extraordinary contributions to the profession.

[Historic Sites in Journalism](link_46)  
The recognition honors individuals, news organizations and places of national historic journalism interest.

[Sunshine Award](link_47)  
The Sunshine Award recognizes those making important contributions in the area of open government.

[[Top]](https://www.spj.org/awards/#)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)National SPJ Honors (Members)

[Howard S. Dubin Outstanding Pro Member Award](link_48)  
The Award salutes individual professional members who have made significant contributions to their SPJ chapter.

[David L. Eshelman Outstanding Campus Adviser Award](link_49)  
The Award honors individuals who have done an outstanding job serving as SPJ campus adviser and who have contributed to their chapters and the national organization over an extended period of time.

[Julie Galvan Outstanding Graduate in Journalism Award](link_50)  
The Award honors a graduating student in journalism who is outstanding in his or her class on the basis of character, service to the community, scholarship, proficiency in practical journalism and significant contributions to their SPJ chapter.

[Robert D.G. Lewis First Amendment Award](link_51)  
This Award honors a student who has demonstrated outstanding service to the First Amendment through the field of journalism.

[Wells Memorial Key](link_52)  
Wells Memorial Key is the highest honor SPJ bestows upon a member for outstanding service to the Society over a period of years.

[[Top]](https://www.spj.org/awards/#)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)National Chapter Awards

[Circle of Excellence Awards](link_53)  
The awards recognize chapters for outstanding efforts in five key areas.

[Outstanding Professional and Campus Chapter Awards](link_54)  
The awards salute chapters for overall excellence in supporting the Society’s missions, members and the profession. Up to three large and three small professional chapters will be selected each year for recognition, with one in each category being chosen as the chapter of the year. On the campus level, one will be selected from each of SPJ’s 12 regions, with one being chosen as the overall campus chapter of the year.

[[Top]](https://www.spj.org/awards/#)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)Local and Regional SPJ Contests

Recognizing outstanding achievement in journalism and dedicated service to the profession and the Society is an important part of the Society of Professional Journalists. The purpose is to stimulate high standards and ethical behavior in the practice of journalism. Many SPJ regions and local chapters have developed their recognition programs to honor individuals and groups for their work, service and contributions to the Society and the profession.

[The Green Eyeshade Awards](link_55)  
Open to journalists in 11 southeastern states: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and West Virginia.

[Northwest Excellence in Journalism Awards](link_56)  
Includes Professional, High School/Community College contests and Scholarships. Sponsored by SPJ Western Washington Pro Chapter.

[Press Club of Long Island Awards](link_57)

[Dateline Awards](link_58)  
Sponsored by the SPJ Washington, D.C. Pro Chapter.

[South Florida Chapter Scholarships](link_59)Must be from South Florida.

[The Golden Press Card Awards](link_60)  
Sponsored by the East Tennessee Pro Chapter.

[Journalist of the Year & Excellence in Journalism](link_61)  
Sponsored by the Metropolitan Detroit Chapter.

[Ohio’s Best Journalism](link_62)  
Conducted jointly by the Cincinnati, Columbus and Cleveland SPJ pro chapters.

[Peter Lisagor Awards for Exemplary Journalism](link_63)Sponsored by the Chicago Headline Club.

[Page One Awards](link_64)  
Sponsored by the SPJ Minnesota Pro Chapter.

[Los Angeles Pro Chapter Annual Awards](link_65)  
For more information, visit this chapter’s website.

[NJ-SPJ Excellence in Journalism Awards](link_66)  
This contest is open to all news outlets who cover New Jersey. Outlets based in New Jersey compete in the Garden State Division. Outlets based in Philadelphia or New York, along with national outlets compete in the Metro Division. Content producers are not required to live in New Jersey.

[[Top]](https://www.spj.org/awards/#)

* * *

## [](https://www.spj.org/awards/)Discontinued Awards

[Bayonet Awards](link_67)  
Recognizing the nation’s edgiest student journalists. Are you sharp enough?

[First Amendment Award](link_68)  
The First Amendment Award honored individuals and organizations for extraordinarily strong efforts to preserve and strengthen the First Amendment.

[Helen Thomas Award](link_69)  
The Helen Thomas Award honored an individual or individuals for a lifetime of contribution to the journalism profession.

[Heroes of the 50 States: The State Government Hall of fame](link_70)  
A joint venture by SPJ and the National Freedom of Information Coalition. It  
was developed by leaders in both organizations as a way to recognize long-term  
contributions of individuals to open government in their respective states.

[Kunkel Awards](link_71)  
SPJ’s Kunkel Awards recognized excellence in video game journalism.

**Pulliam/Kilgore Freedom of Information Internships**The Society of Professional Journalists annually awards two Pulliam/Kilgore Freedom of Information Internships. One intern works in the offices of the Society’s First Amendment legal counsel in Washington, D.C. The other intern works at the Society’s National Headquarters in Indianapolis.

[Regional Director of the Year Award](link_72)  
This Award honored an outstanding SPJ regional director.

[The CCC Awards for College Coronavirus Coverage](link_73)Five major organizations — The Society of Professional Journalists, the Associated Collegiate Press, the Society for News Design, College Broadcasters, Inc., and the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education — have joined forces to recognize college journalists who are admirably covering a pandemic for little or no money while struggling with online classes.

[The Liberty Awards](link_74)  
We want to reward college newspapers that print election editions ahead of the 2024 president election on Tuesday, Nov. 5. Print still has a place on college campuses, and it’s especially effective for previewing big events. And what’s bigger than a presidential election?

# What we do

###### [Our Role: A Voice for Journalists Across the Country: SPJ’s Strategic Priorities Overview](link_53)

* * *

## [We are champions for journalists.](link_54)

[![Image 9](https://www.spj.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/c4-champions-v2.gif)](https://www.spj.org/spjs-core-four-we-are-champions-for-journalists/ [link_54])

*   We recognize the achievements of journalists and best practices of media organizations through our awards programs.
*   We educate journalists on best practices, skills and new innovations.
*   We create products and services that help instill pride of vocation in journalists at all stages in their career.
*   We encourage news organizations to build newsrooms that are diverse, equitable and inclusive.

[Learn More](link_54)

## [We are fighters for the First Amendment.](link_55)

[![Image 10](https://www.spj.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/c4-fighters-v2.gif)](https://www.spj.org/spjs-core-four-we-are-fighters-for-the-first-amendment/ [link_55])

*   We monitor and fight against efforts to violate the First Amendment and suppress free press.
*   We defend journalists through legal defense funds and activate initiatives to protect the First Amendment through our First Amendment Forever Fund.
*   We increase public awareness and support of the First Amendment through training and education.

[Learn More](link_55)

## [We are stewards for ethical journalism.](link_56)

[![Image 11](https://www.spj.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/c4-stewards-v2.gif)](https://www.spj.org/spjs-core-four-we-are-stewards-for-ethical-journalism/ [link_56])

*   We build public trust in the media and greater accountability in the profession via an ethics response team, ethics hotline, and other programming.
*   We promote and advance ethics through a Code of Ethics that is the most widely used code in journalism today.
*   As our Code of Ethics states, we encourage journalists to boldly tell the story of the diversity and magnitude of the human experience.

[Learn More](link_56)

## [We are producers of journalism’s future.](link_57)

[![Image 12](https://www.spj.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/c4-producers-v2.gif)](https://www.spj.org/spjs-core-four-we-are-producers-of-journalisms-future/ [link_57])

*   We proactively design initiatives that amplify new and diverse voices for both SPJ and journalism overall.
*   We provide examination, thought leadership and resources that support a more sustainable future for journalism.
*   We help prepare the next generation of journalists through our student and young professional programs.
*   We embrace, employ and educate journalists on technology and innovation to build journalism’s future.

[Learn More](link_57)

* * *

# What else we’re up to

 June 3, 2026 

# EWA Announces 2025 National Awards for Education Reporting Category Winners

For the full list of category winners, [click here](https://ewa.org/members-news/awards/full-list-2025-education-writers-association-awards-winners).

**Photo credit:** James Minichello for EWA

**June 3, 2026 (WASHINGTON, DC)—**The Education Writers Association is delighted to present the category winners for the 2025 National Awards for Education Reporting, recognizing the top education journalism in the United States.

Covering everything from early childhood to postsecondary education, journalist honorees mined public records, crafted memorable narratives, and built innovative data tools to expand the public’s understanding and awareness on crucial matters impacting students, schools and communities. Winning entries examined the dismantling of the U.S. Department of Education, the fallout of immigration raids, and investigations into school choice programs, special education and inequitable school funding.

EWA announced the category prizes at an awards ceremony during its 79th National Seminar in Baltimore. Each category prize comes with an honorarium of $750.

Judges selected winners from among 349 eligible entries for 17 categories of competition.

More than 100 current and former editors and reporters independently judged the awards competition. Many are past recipients of prestigious journalism awards from EWA and others.

On Thursday, June 4, EWA will honor top-prize winners: The Ronald D. Moskowitz Prize for Outstanding Beat Reporting comes with $2,500, and the Fred M. Hechinger Grand Prize for Distinguished Education Reporting comes with $5,000.

EWA would like to thank all who entered the competition and express our deep gratitude to the busy professionals who volunteered their time to evaluate this year’s many fine entries.

**April 6, 2026 (WASHINGTON, DC)—**The Education Writers Association is pleased to announce the category finalists for the 2025 National Awards for Education Reporting, recognizing the top education journalism in the United States.

The 2025 finalists covered a wide range of local, regional, and national issues from preschool through higher education – including accountability journalism focused on student learning, health, and safety, the impact of immigration enforcement on school communities, and the effects of massive staffing and research cuts at the U.S. Department of Education.

Fifty-four entrants were named as finalists in 17 awards categories. The category winners will be announced on June 3 at EWA’s [79th National Seminar](https://ewa.org/events/upcoming-events/2026-education-writers-association-national-seminar) in Baltimore. Each category award comes with a $750 prize.

Additionally, EWA will honor the top winners during the 2026 National Seminar: The [Ronald Moskowitz Prize for Outstanding Beat Reporting](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards/ronald-moskowitz-prize-for-outstanding-beat-reporting) comes with $2,500, and the [Fred M. Hechinger Grand Prize for Distinguished Education Reporting](https://ewa.org/ewa-awards/fred-m-hechinger-grand-prize-for-distinguished-education-reporting) comes with $5,000.

Judges selected category awards finalists from among 349 e ligible entries for the 17 awards categories. The competition was independently judged by more than 100 current and former editors and reporters, many of whom are past recipients of prestigious journalism awards from EWA and other organizations.

EWA would like to thank everyone who entered the competition and express our deep gratitude to the busy professionals who volunteered hours and hours of their time to evaluate this year’s many fine entries.

# Member Spotlight: Jenny Brundin on 15 Years of Covering Education

**Photo credit:** Photos courtesy of Colorado Public Radio

After three decades in public radio — including 16 years at KUER covering a number of beats, including education, and 15 years as Colorado Public Radio’s education reporter — Jennifer (Jenny) Brundin retired.

A talented and engaging reporter, she won several awards in the Education Writers Association’s National Awards for Education Reporting, The Associated Press Television and Radio Awards, from Public Radio News Directors Incorporated and more.

### ![Image 2](https://ewa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Jenny-1-1.png)

### EWA spoke to Brundin about her career and asked her what drew her to and what kept her excited about education reporting. Here’s what she said:

“What kept me on the education beat for 15 years was realizing that schools are not just policy arenas; they are complex microcosms of society. They contain the full spectrum of the human experience—joy, heartache, innovation, hope, challenge and exhaustion. My goal was always to try to capture those qualities, ensuring my reporting resonated even with audience members who did not have children in the system.

My early career in public radio, covering everything from legislatures to chemical weapons disposal, taught me to be creative and experimental. I brought that same spirit to education, consciously balancing meat-and-potatoes policy coverage with stories of whimsy, delight, and the authentic, often hilarious, lives of students. I believe focusing solely on accountability journalism is an easy path. The real challenge and reward lie in humanizing and telling stories from inside and outside the classroom.”

### ![Image 3](blob:http://localhost/277125f6671dde14b3901f9e2f85ff7d)

### **Brundin also shared how she maintained a sense of curiosity throughout her 15-year tenure at Colorado Public Radio.**

“I committed to producing at least one deep-dive series annually, attempting to balance that ambition with daily and weekly deadlines. “[Teens Under Stress](https://us.list-manage.com/MlUlox9yIJX?e=f20a324de9&c2id=aec73ec376d24f99cf11752905e9c326)” was particularly rewarding. By 2013, I saw how forces like social media were reshaping the classroom. That awareness led to a 2019 series, when my colleagues and I interviewed 100 teens about how climate change, academic and parental pressure, and other stressors were converging into a youth mental health crisis.”

### **Brundin spoke about burnout in journalism and gave tips for protecting one’s long-term capacity.**

“The sheer volume of this beat is daunting, especially in public radio, where you are balancing and must produce distinct radio, digital, and visual stories. Over time, I learned that “feeding the beast” can lead to burnout (which got me in the end!).

My best advice for longevity is to set boundaries. Use resources like EWA to navigate the complexities, study the stellar work of peers for inspiration, but always prioritize your specific audience. Do the work you can manage well, find the stories that truly matter, and protect your sanity along the way.”

The Sigma Delta Chi Awards date back to 1932, when the Society first honored six individuals for contributions to journalism. The current program began in 1939, when the organization awarded the first Distinguished Service Awards. These awards later became the Sigma Delta Chi Awards.

The awards recognize the best in professional journalism in [categories](https://www.spj.org/a-sdx-categories.asp) covering print/online, audio, television, and more.

New streamlined awards portal for easier contest entry.

* * *

## General Rules

*   The contest is open to any work published or broadcast by a U.S. or international media outlet in 2025. Freelance work is eligible. Every entry must be accompanied by a one-page cover letter.
*   Apart from Spanish-language categories, if not originally published or broadcast in English, entries must include an English transcript or English subtitles.
*   [All entries in all categories must be uploaded to the online awards site.](https://go.spj.org/awards-enter?award=SDX)
*   Entrants in all online categories should keep their sites intact and accessible until September 30, 2026.
*   Divisions within a category might be combined during judging, depending on the number of entries. Entries may be reassigned to appropriate categories by contest administrators.
*   Up to four (4) individuals may be named on a team entry. Otherwise, the entry must be made in the name of the staff of the publication or station.
*   No part of any entry will be returned. SPJ reserves the right to use any part or the whole of any entry for publicity, educational or promotional purposes.
*   If a State/Local news organization collaborates with a National/Network news organization, the entry belongs in a National/Network category.

[[ Back to top ]](https://www.spj.org/sigma-delta-chi-awards/#)

* * *

## Helpful Hints

*   Let your cover letter speak for you. Explain why your entry may be the finest example of journalism in its category. Links to sidebars, editorials, op-ed pieces and letters-to-the-editor may be included in the cover letter.
*   Entries submitted in the wrong category will be disqualified. Entry fees are not refundable.
*   In the Audio/TV categories, all edits/segments should be made explicit, through use of silence, beeps or some other fully transparent mechanism.
*   Print circulation distinctions for newspapers and magazines are to be based on non-Sunday, single-issue distribution. If submitting for a weekly, monthly, or Sunday-only publication, provide single-issue circulation details in the cover letter.

[[ Back to top ]](https://www.spj.org/sigma-delta-chi-awards/#)

## Entry Requirements

#### Entry Fee

Not an SPJ member? Now’s the perfect time to join. [Join today and save on your entry fee.](https://www.spj.org/become-a-member/)

**SPJ members**

*   Early bird rate: $65 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Jan. 6, 2026
*   Regular rate: $80 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Feb. 18, 2026

**Non-members**

*   Regular rate: $115 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Feb. 18, 2026
*   Extended rate: $115 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Feb. 25, 2026

To claim the member fee, you must supply your personal SPJ member number. A team may use the member fee if any of its members belongs to SPJ. Provide the member’s name and SPJ member number.

*   SPJ accepts credit card payments via Stripe.
*   Make checks payable to Society of Professional Journalists.
*   No refunds issued.
*   Please note: SPJ does not have institutional memberships for professional organizations, in which one membership number would cover all entries.

* * *

#### Cover Letter

A one-page cover letter must be provided with an entry. If the entry is in a circulation- or market-divided category, include that information. Use non-Sunday, single-issue distribution for print circulation. If submitting for a weekly, monthly or Sunday-only publication, provide single-issue circulation details.

In addition, the letter could include:

*   A summary of the entry.
*   A discussion of major findings and subsequent results.
*   What it took to get the story, including circumstances; time to report, write and edit; and sources and references used.

* * *

#### Divisions

*   Each entry in divided categories must be accompanied by a statement of the news organization’s coverage area and print circulation, with the name and title of the person submitting. No entry for a divided category will be accepted without a statement of coverage area.
*   Nationally syndicated cable television programs are classified as networks.
*   National/Network and State/Local classifications are based on primary coverage.

* * *

#### Accuracy Requirement

Any corrections, clarifications or retractions made after publishing or broadcast must be submitted with the entry. Include written challenges the entrant or news organization received and the news organization’s response.

Any questions we email back to the entrant will say “URGENT” in the subject field. Please answer promptly.

[[ Back to top ]](https://www.spj.org/sigma-delta-chi-awards/#)

* * *

## Judging Criteria

*   Materials will be judged by a panel of professional journalists and/or journalism educators. All decisions are final except if additional information comes to light after judging.
*   A maximum of one award is issued in each category. There are no ties or honorable mentions.
*   If judges decide no entry merits recognition in that category, no award will be given.
*   If you are unaware of your radio or TV market ranking, check the following links[for radio](https://www.nielsen.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2024/04/Populations_Rankings.pdf?fbclid=IwAR35iULZsQEpz3HHCib_gaWNZQy5cUG1fqeDKcxJK6is-pVve_nRE_0d0b8_aem_ASCUrbIXGLuHEyIrgKaCmCzbbShQylvq6KHQObaHRXl8O8gpqCfS1_01nNUHmsZNaf1McPitESH8WVlBuvHtsEGj) and[for television](https://www.stationindex.com/tv/tv-markets#google_vignette).
*   Local radio and TV stations entering the contest **must** provide their call letters on the entry form.
*   For publication circulation figures, consult your publisher or ad department. Please include relevant information in your cover letter.
*   Each entry must include a source or contact person to verify the news organization’s primary coverage. Each print entry must include a source who can verify circulation.

Entries will be judged on the following criteria:

*   Readability
*   Effectiveness of interpretation
*   Accuracy and completeness
*   Enterprise
*   Clarity and style
*   Resourcefulness of the reporter in overcoming obstacles
*   Interest
*   Alignment with ideas put forth in the SPJ Code of Ethics

*   Entrants need to submit a link to the online article or a PDF of the page on which the story appeared. The date of publication must be visible. Online entries that do not provide complete and accurate URLs will be disqualified.
*   PDFs should have the same name as the title of the story.
*   PDFs should be combined into one file, when possible. The cover letter should be separate from the main entry.
*   Daily publications must be printed at least four times per week. Otherwise, they are considered Non-Daily.
*   Entrants must keep their entries intact and accessible until September 30, 2026.
*   Affiliated online publications are owned by or partnered with media organizations whose primary outlets are not based on the web, such as broadcast stations, newspapers or magazines.
*   Independent online publications are stand-alone sites not owned or partnered with print or broadcast media organizations.
*   Newsletter entrants should submit PDFs of the newsletter issues to be considered.
*   Submit reviews and critical pieces to Cultural Criticism, not the Arts/Fashion Journalism category.

#### Art/Graphics Entries

*   For photography categories, entrant should submit a PDF of the page on which the art appeared in print or a link to the art published on an online news site. The date of publication must be visible.

The Society of Professional Journalists is pleased to announce the recipients of the 2025 Sigma Delta Chi Awards for excellence in journalism.

Judges chose the winners from entries in categories covering print, radio, television and online. The awards recognize outstanding work published or broadcast in 2025.

Dating back to 1932, the awards originally honored six individuals for contributions to journalism. The current program began in 1939, when the Society granted the first Distinguished Service Awards. The honors later became the Sigma Delta Chi Awards.

Founded in 1909 as Sigma Delta Chi, SPJ promotes the free flow of information vital to a well-informed citizenry; works to inspire and educate the next generation of journalists; and protects First Amendment guarantees of freedom of speech and press.

##### Annually, the Society of Professional Journalists presents the Mark of Excellence Awards, honoring the best in student journalism.

Categories are first judged on the regional level. First-place regional winners advance to the national competition, and most are recognized at their respective regional SPJ conference. National winners will be showcased on spj.org.

The Corbin Gwaltney Award for Best Student Newspaper carries a $5,000 prize for each of the large- and small-division winners, courtesy of the Chronicle of Higher Education.

* * *

## Eligibility

*   The contest is open to anyone enrolled in a U.S. or international college or university in 2025, while studying for an academic degree. Students who have had full-time professional journalism experience, outside of internships, by the time their work is completed are ineligible. Work performed as a paid freelancer or part-time employee is not eligible. A group entry that includes any work by someone with full-time professional experience will be disqualified.
*   The entrant must have been enrolled as a student when the work was completed. It may be published or aired post-graduation.
*   Work published or broadcast while working as a student intern is acceptable provided the cover letter states that the overwhelming majority of the work was done by the student and wasn’t heavily edited by a professional.
*   Unpublished manuscripts, classroom exercises (assigned for a grade or to fulfill a course requirement) and unaired news broadcasts do not qualify. That work is not eligible for an MOE Award unless it was also distributed outside the class via common media channels (i.e., published in a student newspaper, distributed on magazine racks, etc.).
*   Advisers may enter for students. An entry fee is based on whether the**student** is an SPJ member.
*   All entries must have been first published or broadcast in 2025.
*   An entry may not include the work of students from more than one school.
*   New this year: Each work may be submitted in multiple appropriate categories, but can only win in one.

[[ Back to Top ]](https://www.spj.org/mark-of-excellence-awards/#)

* * *

## General Rules

*   A one-page cover letter must state school enrollment (for multi-campus schools, use the overall undergraduate and graduate enrollment for that campus). The cover letter should also verify (where applicable) that the research, reporting, writing, photography (video and digital), design and layout were all student produced. It may include a statement and/or links showing the impact of the work. An entry without a cover letter may be disqualified.
*   Winning entries may be reproduced or posted on the SPJ website.
*   There is no limit on the number of entries a school, news outlet or individual may enter.
*   Each entry must be accompanied by the correct entry fee.
*   Be sure the name of each student who worked on the entry is listed on the entry form and spelled correctly.
*   A maximum of four people can be named on a team entry. Otherwise, the entry must be submitted in the name of the news organization.
*   Work will automatically be submitted to the region where the entrant is enrolled in school. International entries are each assigned to one of SPJ’s 12 regions, and international students should (if applicable) indicate an affiliated U.S. school or other regional connection for the entrant. If not applicable, the entry will be randomly assigned to a region.
*   Large and small divisions within a category might be combined during judging, depending on the number of entries. Contest administrators may reassign an entry to an appropriate category, but entrants are responsible for entering their work correctly.
*   Entries not originally published or broadcast in English must include English subtitles or an English translation.
*   Entries that are incomplete or entered in the wrong division or category will be disqualified as soon as the error is discovered. Entrants will not be notified of disqualification and their entry fees will not be refunded.

* * *

#### School Enrollment

*   The Large and Small divisions are classified by total campuswide student enrollment, which includes full-time and part-time, both undergraduate and graduate. It is not based on a) just a journalism school or b) multiple campuses added together.
*   Each cover letter MUST include the school’s enrollment and a person to contact to verify that information.

* * *

#### Submitting Your MOE Award Entry

[All entries in every category must be uploaded to the online awards site.](https://go.spj.org/awards-enter?award=MOE)

* * *

#### Accuracy Requirement

Any corrections, clarifications, retractions made after initial publishing or broadcast must be submitted as part of the entry, along with any written challenges the news organization received about the report’s fairness or accuracy. Responses by the news organization should be included. Please include this information in the one-page cover letter with appropriate links.

* * *

#### Fees

Not an SPJ member? Now’s the perfect time to join. [Join today and save 50 percent on your entry fee.](http://go.spj.org/member-join)

**SPJ members**

*   Early bird rate: $30 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Jan. 6, 2026
*   Regular rate: $35 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Feb. 11, 2026

**Non-members**

*   Early bird rate: $40 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Jan. 6, 2026
*   Regular rate: $45 per entry until 11:59 p.m. ET Feb. 11, 2026

*   Each submission by an SPJ member must have the appropriate entry fee and the entrant’s membership number. Do not use another student’s membership number to obtain the member entry fee.
*   When an entry by more than one person is submitted, the member fee applies if at least one team member belongs to SPJ. The member must be identified and supply their membership number. An adviser’s membership number may not be used for any entry.
*   For the Best All-Around categories, the editor must be a member to use the lower fee. You must supply the editor’s name and membership number.
*   SPJ accepts credit card payments via Stripe.
*   **Make checks and money orders payable to:**Society of Professional Journalists. Check payments must include the award confirmation number in the memo line. Multiple confirmation numbers should be listed on a note accompanying the check.
*   No refunds will be issued.

* * *

#### Judging/Criteria

Judging will be based on overall excellence. Criteria include:

*   Accuracy and completeness
*   Enterprise and ingenuity
*   Adherence to high journalistic standards
*   Significance and effectiveness
*   Extenuating circumstances
*   Clarity, insight and respect for the audience
*   Creative use of the medium’s unique capabilities
*   Ethical principles outlined in the SPJ Code of Ethics
*   Available resources

One winner and up to two finalists will be chosen in each category unless the judges find that the entries do not meet the overall standard of excellence required. No ties or honorable mentions will be awarded. A winner must be named in a category if there are finalists.

#### Print/Online

*   Entrants must submit a link to the online article or a PDF of the newspaper/magazine page on which the story appeared. The date of publication must be visible.
*   PDFs must have the same name as the title of the story and be combined into one file, when possible. Word documents containing the work will not be accepted.
*   Entries should include a cover letter verifying that all research, reporting, writing, photography (video and digital), design and layout was student produced. Failure to include this letter could result in disqualification.
*   Entrants must keep their entries intact and accessible until September 30, 2026.
*   Regional judging will take place February-April 2026. Best Affiliated Website and Best Independent Online Student Publication categories will be judged on content as presented during this time span.

* * *

#### Art/Graphics/Multimedia

*   For photographs published in a newspaper or magazine or on an online news site.
*   Entrant should submit a PDF of the news/magazine page on which the art appeared in print, or a link to the art published on an online news site. The date of publication should be visible.
*   For single-photo categories, it is OK to include the entire piece, but make clear which photo to judge. If possible, attach it separately.
*   Entries should include a cover letter verifying that the work was all student produced. Failure to include this letter could result in disqualification.
*   Video entries must have been broadcast by a campus, public or commercial television station or franchised cable television system or through streaming media.
*   Online/digital entries shall come from websites, areas of websites and all digital platforms operated by a campus affiliated organization or program. It also may be published on a third-party site, such as YouTube, as long as the work was done for a news organization.

The Society of Professional Journalists is pleased to announce the national winners of the 2025 Mark of Excellence Awards, recognizing collegiate work published or broadcast during 2025.

The awards honor the best in student journalism. As such, judges were directed to choose only those entries which they felt were outstanding work worthy of a national honor. If the judges determined that none of the entries rose to the level of excellence, no award was given. Any category not listed has no winner.

School divisions are based on student enrollment, which includes both graduate and undergraduate enrollment. Schools with more than 10,000 students are designated as large schools.

National Mark of Excellence Award judges can choose up to one national winner in each category and two national finalists (runners-up).

Winners and finalists were previously recognized by receiving first-place in one of the SPJ’s 12 regional competitions. Each first-place regional winner advanced to the national competition.

* * *

# Students and Educators: Let SPJ help guide the way

The Society of Professional Journalists understands that changes in the industry have forced educators to rethink and revise curricula. They are being asked — or required — to help students learn about everything that’s new while still teaching the reporting and writing skills that serve as the foundation of journalism. Institutions of higher learning are breaking their budgets to keep up with new software, new hardware and new gadgets. The job of a journalism educator is more demanding than ever before.

Just know that you are not alone. And the Society of Professional Journalists is there to help.

* * *

#### By becoming a member of SPJ:

*   We can connect you with experts in reporting, writing, ethics, diversity, freedom of expression, open government, freelancing and, yes, media technology.
*   We provide a chance for your students to work alongside our professional members. This is because our students are full members, complete with the same benefits as our professional members. (Two students even serve on our national board of directors.)
*   We keep students updated on the industry through local and regional professional development programs, and publications such as our weekly e-newsletter “SPJ Leads” and our member magazine “Quill.”
*   We connect your students to the organization with the best-known journalism code of ethics in the world. (It’s been translated into 11 languages.)

* * *

The best way for SPJ to serve your students is for your school to start a campus chapter. This would encourage your students to work together to provide locally relevant, SPJ-sponsored programming that will enhance their education. It is easy to set up a campus chapter; [you can find out how by visiting this page.](https://www.spj.org/start-an-spj-campus-chapter/)

If a campus chapter isn’t something you can do right now, we ask that you still encourage your students to join SPJ. This will give them an opportunity to network with other student and professional members. And if you have a professional chapter nearby, your students may be able to join their group.

Joining is easy and affordable; students pay only $40 for annual dues (cheaper than most textbooks) or $105 for a four-year membership if the student is a freshman or sophomore. [You can learn more about becoming an SPJ member, and download applications, by following this link.](https://www.spj.org/become-a-member)

Your school can also show its dedication to journalism is by joining SPJ as a collegiate institutional member. In doing so, your school will demonstrate to students (and parents) its commitment to producing the best journalists possible. For just $400 a year, your school can join SPJ as a Collegiate Institutional Member. Please share this information with your journalism department leaders.

* * *

#### Our Collegiate Institutional Members receive:

##### Thank you to our existing members

[Learn more about SPJ’s Collegiate Institutional Memberships, and see a list of schools who have pledged their support and commitment to SPJ and journalism.](https://www.spj.org/become-a-collegiate-institutional-member/)

*   Your name on SPJ.org’s [Collegiate Institutional Membership page](https://www.spj.org/become-a-collegiate-institutional-member/) that links to your school’s Web site.
*   A subscription to Quill Magazine.
*   A $5 discount on individual memberships for students and professionals from your school. This benefit will help you in building a chapter on your campus.
*   A complimentary entry in SPJ’s Mark of Excellence Contest, which honors the best in student journalism from across the country.
*   A framed copy of SPJ’s Code of Ethics and several pocket-sized copies of the Code.
*   A complimentary convention registration to SPJ’s National Convention (a savings of nearly $200).

* * *

The best part is your school doesn’t need to have a campus SPJ chapter to become a Collegiate Institutional Member. And it’s one of the easiest ways to expose your students to the largest journalism organization in the country.

# Member Spotlight: Jenny Brundin on 15 Years of Covering Education

**Photo credit:** Photos courtesy of Colorado Public Radio

After three decades in public radio — including 16 years at KUER covering a number of beats, including education, and 15 years as Colorado Public Radio’s education reporter — Jennifer (Jenny) Brundin retired.

A talented and engaging reporter, she won several awards in the Education Writers Association’s National Awards for Education Reporting, The Associated Press Television and Radio Awards, from Public Radio News Directors Incorporated and more.

### ![Image 2](https://ewa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Jenny-1-1.png)

### EWA spoke to Brundin about her career and asked her what drew her to and what kept her excited about education reporting. Here’s what she said:

“What kept me on the education beat for 15 years was realizing that schools are not just policy arenas; they are complex microcosms of society. They contain the full spectrum of the human experience—joy, heartache, innovation, hope, challenge and exhaustion. My goal was always to try to capture those qualities, ensuring my reporting resonated even with audience members who did not have children in the system.

My early career in public radio, covering everything from legislatures to chemical weapons disposal, taught me to be creative and experimental. I brought that same spirit to education, consciously balancing meat-and-potatoes policy coverage with stories of whimsy, delight, and the authentic, often hilarious, lives of students. I believe focusing solely on accountability journalism is an easy path. The real challenge and reward lie in humanizing and telling stories from inside and outside the classroom.”

### ![Image 3](blob:http://localhost/277125f6671dde14b3901f9e2f85ff7d)

### **Brundin also shared how she maintained a sense of curiosity throughout her 15-year tenure at Colorado Public Radio.**

“I committed to producing at least one deep-dive series annually, attempting to balance that ambition with daily and weekly deadlines. “[Teens Under Stress](https://us.list-manage.com/MlUlox9yIJX?e=f20a324de9&c2id=aec73ec376d24f99cf11752905e9c326)” was particularly rewarding. By 2013, I saw how forces like social media were reshaping the classroom. That awareness led to a 2019 series, when my colleagues and I interviewed 100 teens about how climate change, academic and parental pressure, and other stressors were converging into a youth mental health crisis.”

### **Brundin spoke about burnout in journalism and gave tips for protecting one’s long-term capacity.**

“The sheer volume of this beat is daunting, especially in public radio, where you are balancing and must produce distinct radio, digital, and visual stories. Over time, I learned that “feeding the beast” can lead to burnout (which got me in the end!).

My best advice for longevity is to set boundaries. Use resources like EWA to navigate the complexities, study the stellar work of peers for inspiration, but always prioritize your specific audience. Do the work you can manage well, find the stories that truly matter, and protect your sanity along the way.”

# Awards Announced for Outstanding Education Journalism in ’99

March 08, 2000  3 min read

*   Share article
*   Remove Save to favorites Save to favorites 
*   [Print](javascript:window.print())

[Email](mailto:?body=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03%0A%0A%0AArticles%20on%20testing%2C%20desegregation%2C%20and%20early-childhood%20education%20are%20among%20the%20winners%20of%20the%201999%20National%20Awards%20for%20Education%20Reporting%2C%20announced%20last%20week%20by%20the%20Education%20Writers%20Association.)[Facebook](link_71)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03&mini=true&title=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999&summary=%0AArticles%20on%20testing%2C%20desegregation%2C%20and%20early-childhood%20education%20are%20among%20the%20winners%20of%20the%201999%20National%20Awards%20for%20Education%20Reporting%2C%20announced%20last%20week%20by%20the%20Education%20Writers%20Association.&source=Education%20Week)[Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03&text=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999)Copy URL

Articles on testing, desegregation, and early-childhood education are among the winners of the 1999 National Awards for Education Reporting, announced last week by the Education Writers Association.

The awards, honoring coverage of education by print and broadcast journalists, were chosen from 459 entries and were selected by a panel of reporters, editors, college professors, and educators.

First-place winners will receive $250 and a plaque. Second-place winners will receive a certificate.

## For You

[![Image 2](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1c038c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1440x960+0+0/resize/945x630!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fa5%2F60%2F1c4345d64367a98d09521323b80d%2F110724-symonds-elem-nh-13-sp-bs.jpg)](https://www.edweek.org/education/awards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99/2000/03#promo)

[Student Well-Being](link_12)[From Our Research Center](link_72)[Why School Isn't Working for Many Boys and What Could Help](link_73)[Teachers report in a new survey that boys are less focused and engaged than their female counterparts.](link_73)

An overall award chosen from among the winners, the Fred M. Hechinger Grand Prize for Distinguished Education Reporting, will be presented at the EWA’s annual convention in Atlanta next month.

_Education Week_ received a special citation in the special interest/trade publication category, to which the newspaper is assigned, for its yearlong series about the development of public education over the past 100 years, _Lessons of a Century_. The winning entry in that category was an article, [“Generation of Cheaters,”](link_74) by Kevin Bushweller, in the _American School Board Journal._

Other first-place winners are:

**Newspapers over 100,000 circulation:**

Breaking news: “Deciding Desegregation,” by Celeste Smith, Debbie Cenziper, Jennifer Wing Rothacker, and Ted Mellnik, _The Charlotte_ (N.C.) _Observer_.

**Features:** “A Life’s Lesson,” by Chris Moran, _The San Diego Union-Tribune._

**News feature or issue package:** “Educating Alex,” by John Gittelsohn and Bruce Chambers, _The Orange County_ (Calif.) _Register_.

**Series or group of articles:** “Worlds Apart,” by Tim Simmons, _The News & Observer_, Raleigh, N.C.

**Investigative reporting:** “Dirty Secrets,” by Jane Elizabeth Zemel and Steve Twedt, the _Pittsburgh Post-Gazette._

**Opinion:** “Early Childhood Well-Being,” by Linda Valdez, _The Arizona Republic_, Phoenix.

**Special section or page:** “3 to 6: The Teen Alone Zone,” by Kate Taylor, Lisa Daniels, Robin Franzen, Gillian Gaynair, Spencer Heinz, Romel Hernandez, Inara Verzemnieks, Chris Broderick, and Susan Gage, _The Oregonian_, Portland.

**Newspapers under 100,000 circulation:**

Breaking news: “A War Over Words,” by Jennifer Rose Marino, the _Savannah_ (Ga.) _Morning News_.

**Features:** “No Way Out,” by Kathryn C. Eastburn, _Colorado Springs_ (Colo.) _Independent_.

**News feature or issue package:** “None of the Above,” by Nigel Jaquiss _, Willamette Week_, Portland, Ore.

**Series or group of articles:** “Reinventing Our Public Schools,” by Marjorie Coeyman, Stephanie Cook, Mark Clayton, and Gail Russell Chaddock, _The Christian Science Monitor._

**Investigative reporting (tie):** “A System Padded With Patronage,” by Sean Patrick Lyons and staff, _Waterbury_ (Conn.) _Republican-American_; and “Investigation of University of Colorado President,” by Brian Hansen, Pamela White, Terje Langeland, Mark Collins, and Amanda Hill, _Colorado Daily_, University of Colorado at Boulder.

**Opinion:** “Rx for taas,” by John P. Young, _Waco_ (Texas) _Tribune-Herald_.

**Special section or page:** “Heralding the New Millennium,” by Carol Trapani, Kathleen Norton, Dolores Pinto, John A. Torres, Michelle Vellucci, and others, _Poughkeepsie_ (N.Y.) _Journal_.

**Magazines**

National magazine article: “Schooling the Imagination,” by Todd Oppenheimer, _The_ _Atlantic Monthly_.

**Regional/local magazine article:** “Hitting the Books,” by Jennifer O’Donnell, _Tidewater Parent_, Virginia Beach, Va.

**Broadcast**

Hard news and investigative coverage, television: “Teacher Shortage: False Alarm?,” by John Merrow, John D. Tulenko, Ivan Crowther, and Merill Stern, “The Merrow Report,” PBS.

**Documentary and feature, TV:** “Secrets of the SAT,” by Michael Chandler and Sharon Tiller, WGBH Frontline West, Berkeley, Calif.

**Radio:** “Education Reform,” by Kathryn Baron, KQED-FM, San Francisco.

**—Alan Richard**

A version of this article appeared in the _March 08, 2000_ edition of _Education Week_ as _Awards Announced for Outstanding Education Journalism in ’99_

At Education Week, we believe that all children deserve a high-quality education. Guided by this vision, we make it our mission to empower the entire education community, from educators and policymakers to business leaders and beyond. As an expert source of news and opinion, research and analysis, events, and more, we cover issues across the field—offering deeper insights and actionable resources, so our audiences can create a stronger tomorrow for all students.

[Learn More](link_70)

[![Image 5: EdWeek Our People](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3f1f1b4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2700x1799+0+4/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc9%2F22%2Ff64063f742cf8235d65b3fbed313%2Fedweek-our-people.jpg)](https://www.edweek.org/about/our-people [link_69])

Building Comprehensive Knowledge

Education Week is the #1 source of non-partisan, high-quality news, and insights covering the K-12 education sector. Specializing in education, the seasoned journalists on our full-time newsroom staff have worked for many of the country’s leading media outlets, including The Washington Post, ABC News, and The Los Angeles Times.  
  
Enhanced by our thorough, independent research and analysis, the Education Week newsroom covers stories across the entire education sphere. As a result, not only do we provide content that helps district and school leaders do their job better, our work continues to be cited regularly in state and federal policymaking, including Supreme Court decisions."

[Learn About our Editorial Team](link_69)

# Lynn (Yunfei) Liu

Follow Unfollow

Digital News Specialist, Education Week 

Lynn (Yunfei) Liu is a digital news specialist for Education Week, where she produces five flagship newsletters, curates multimedia content, and participates in efforts to rethink or improve our digital news strategies. Before joining Education Week, she earned a master’s degree in journalism from Medill, Northwestern University. She also interned at Open Campus and NBC.

We Are Our People

Expertise defines us, Passion drives us. As the nation’s premier publisher of K-12 news, analysis, and information, Education Week’s reporters, editors, researchers, and management have vast expertise in the field, with in-depth knowledge of school-related issues and data, education policy and practice, and the news industry at large.  
  
Our staff experts are available for media interviews and panel participation on the topics below. To contact our experts, email them individually or call 301-280-3100 and ask for the Managing Editor.

[CONTACT US](https://www.edweek.org/contact/)

## Our Leaders

*   ## Michele J. Givens

President and CEO

Michele Givens is an experienced and strategically focused publishing executive who has helped lead the nonprofit media organization, best known for publishing Education Week, in a time of profound and often difficult change.

She joined EPE as general manager in 2001 and formally received the concurrent title of publisher in 2009. In June 2016, the EPE Board of Trustees announced her appointment to succeed her longtime colleague Virginia B. Edwards as the organization’s president and CEO, effective August 1, 2016.

Previously in her career, Givens was the consumer marketing director for Outside magazine in Santa Fe, N.M.; associate consumer marketing manager at Rodale Press in Emmaus, Pa.; and circulation director at McGraw-Hill in Washington, D.C.

Givens earned an M.S. in the Management of Information Technology from the University of Virginia, an M.B.A. from the University of New Mexico, and a bachelor’s degree from George Mason University.

She serves on the board of directors of the Center for Teaching Quality and is a member of the National Press Club.  ![Image 3: Michele Givens](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b837ba/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3164x4768+0+0/resize/215x324!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F07%2Ffb%2Fb7e8ac66477c93e0a1cd139aef68%2Fmichele-givens-2-jb.jpg)      
*   * * *   
## Beth Frerking

Editor-in-Chief

Beth Frerking, a veteran journalist and newsroom leader who has worked as a top editor, reporter, and journalism educator, currently serves as editor-in-chief for Education Week.

Frerking’s achievements include being named a magazine innovator by the [Folio: 100 Awards](https://archive.foliomag.com/events/folio-100-awards-networking-reception-2017/) and two National Headliner awards for her work covering children, families, and education. While at The Dallas Times Herald,she was part of a reporting team that covered the crash of Delta Flight 191. This work was a finalist for the [Pulitzer Prize in Public Service](https://www.pulitzer.org/finalists/staff-28).

Her other accomplishments include helping to launch and oversee the Education Lab, a community-funded reporting team created to expand in-depth education coverage at The Dallas Morning News, and helping to establish The Politico Network, a content-sharing network that included more than 100 news organizations, two-thirds of which were newspapers.

Frerking’s previous experience includes editor-in-chief of The National Law Journal;senior editor and assistant managing editor at Politico; news vertical editor at The Dallas Morning News; national correspondent for the former Newhouse News Service; Washington bureau chief and congressional correspondent for The Denver Post; director of the Journalism Center on Children & Families, previously part of the Philip Merrill College of Journalism at the University of Maryland, and editor of The Daily Texan.

Frerking is an honors graduate of University of Texas at Austin’s School of Journalism.       ![Image 4: Beth Frerking](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/371f09b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3354x5054+15+0/resize/215x324!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc7%2Fdb%2F094a12a348fa9a3e8f8f40b5bb9b%2Fbeth-frerking-jb.jpg)
