![Image 2: EdWeek Our Story](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ba496e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2700x969+0+419/resize/1463x525!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F78%2F8e%2F79109b824392bcc656953f247dc0%2Fedweek-our-story.jpg)

Gwen Keraval for Education Week

Today Education Week is recognized as the premier source of news, information, and analysis on K-12 education. But our origins are in the Sputnik era, when anxiety over the United States’ ability to withstand a concerted challenge to its technological pre-eminence touched off a wave of initiatives to improve the nation’s schools and colleges. In 1957, a bold experiment by 15 editors of leading university alumni magazines to speak with one voice to their readers as higher education sought to respond to the deep national concerns of that time. And this is where our story begins:

![Image 3: Operation Moonshooter, Minutes of the Organizational Meeting, Jan. 12, 1957   Series 1.1, Box 1, Folder 1 1](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bada610/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2550x1699+0+0/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc6%2F05%2F9762c49d49c896da355c18f745bf%2Foperation-moonshooter-minutes-of-the-organizational-meeting-jan.%2012%2C%201957%20-%20Series%201.1%2C%20Box%201%2C%20Folder%201-1.jpg)

1957

The Soviet Union’s 1957 launch of the first manmade satellite to orbit the earth riveted attention on space and inspired the editors to call their collaborative research and writing project the “Moonshooter.” With a $12,000 grant from the Carnegie Corporation of New York, they produced a report the next year formally titled American Higher Education: 1958. Eventually, 150 colleges signed up for the 32-page report, which reached nearly 1 million college-educated Americans.  
  
The success of that first venture led to the group’s incorporation as Editorial Projects in Education, a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization, and the production of further reports and publications oriented to higher education. The most notable of those endeavors was The Chronicle of Higher Education. Launched in November 1966, on the eve of an extraordinarily turbulent period for America’s university campuses, The Chronicle was soon recognized as an unparalleled observer of the higher education scene.

![Image 4: merlin 137812695 dadf7775 a3a2 4ce4 9671 38b2c95cda60 superJumbo](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b6fcdf9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1371x913+0+230/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F0c%2F3d%2F8be3ef4e44ae90b52efa6306aaba%2Fmerlin-137812695-dadf7775-a3a2-4ce4-9671-38b2c95cda60-superjumbo.jpg)

1978

In 1978, EPE sold The Chronicle to its editors—a decision that set the stage for a fundamental shift in direction by EPE to pre-K-12 education. Inspired by the example of The Chronicle, EPE determined that the precollegiate field likewise needed independent, first-rate journalistic coverage of national scope.

![Image 5: EW Vol 1 Issue 1 (9 7 81) 1](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/20617bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3480x2318+0+46/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fe0%2Fb7%2F19cbc5074bf1bfaa24c625f3bdca%2Few-vol-1-issue-1-9-7-81-1.jpg)

1981

Education Week was first published by EPE in September 1981 with just 18 employees and the support again of the Carnegie Corporation as well as other philanthropies.

![Image 6: charles0000170A](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a6e6aa8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7114x4739+0+23/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fa1%2Fec%2F76cd8c2c4754a2b61a1bc7d6ae4e%2Fcharles0000170a.jpg)

1983

Just as the launch of The Chronicle had occurred on the cusp of an epochal period for higher education, the debut of the “chronicle of precollegiate education” came as the first stirrings of a remarkable age of ferment in elementary and secondary policy were being felt. And even as Education Week’s early issues were airing the still-new Reagan administration’s plans to curtail the federal role in education, the field’s upstart “newspaper of record” was pointing to new anxieties about the state of the nation’s schools that echoed those of EPE’s earliest days. Those concerns, emerging against a backdrop of global competition and economic dislocation, gained rhetorical force and political momentum with the 1983 federal report A Nation at Risk.

![Image 7: firstsite](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/481c18d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1621x1080+149+0/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc6%2F0e%2Fa5b1840f41b797792bb293c47190%2Ffirstsite.jpg)

1996

Launch of edweek.org ushered EPE into the Digital Age and created a platform for the evolution of its Education Week flagship publication into an integrated print-digital news organization that provides distinctive staff-written original reporting, a forum for a lively but civil exchange of opinion on education issues, an unequaled online archive of 30-plus years of education coverage, high-quality content from news and information partners, interactive databases, and a host of video, multimedia, and other features that clarify complex points of policy and bring the stories of American schools, educators, students, and parents to life

![Image 8: EPE staff at the DC office on Connecticut Ave. near Van Ness (UDC) approximately mid 1990s.](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4af3660/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3498x2330+0+110/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fa5%2F90%2Ff8b150cb40edb75b551c8d3dce7e%2Fedwstaff-old.jpg)

1998

The company moves to Bethesda, Md., just outside Washington DC.

![Image 9: Alyson Kelin and Andrew Ujifusa Inside the Newsroom Closeup](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2a49953/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4000x2665+0+1/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F2c%2Fd2%2F86c862ac45e4906fa3222a71c682%2Falyson-kelin-and-andrew-ujifusa-inside-the-newsroom-closeup.jpg)

2002-2015

The ensuing waves of K-12 improvement measures known simply as “the reform movement” helped establish, in turn, Education Week’s role as the most trusted source of news and analysis on one of the biggest continuing stories in American society. That role took on fresh importance as Education Week tracked the far-reaching No Child Left Behind Act, signed into law in 2002, and now the implementation of its 2015 successor, the Every Student Succeeds Act.

![Image 10: QC002](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4a90878/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1399+0+1/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc3%2F33%2Fef578ea548ad8aa278b3cc3e9e56%2Fqc002.jpg)

2010

Education Week introduces a new series of special reports testifying to the time-tested value of print. At the same time, edweek.org employs a variety of digital tools to allow readers of a special report to delve deeper into its findings or explore the topic through online storytelling. Included in Education Week’s lineup of print editions are three high-profile annual reports—Quality Counts, Technology Counts, and Leaders To Learn From—and a mix of popular reports on such subjects as literacy instruction, personalized learning, student assessment, school principals, and teacher professional development.

![Image 11: Maurice Bakely, publisher of Ed Week Market Brief, at the EdMarketer event in 2019 in Boulder, Co.](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b40474b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6589x4389+0+2/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F8d%2Fc6%2Fa85abc974f66bbcacced02206739%2Flead7975.jpg)

2015

EPE launched EdWeek Market Brief, its first premium, membership-based information service. The online-only EdWeek Market Brief provides original data and actionable intelligence and analysis that aim to bridge the knowledge gap between pre-K-12-serving companies and the needs of schools and districts.

![Image 12: Video Team](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5c682f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3960x2638+0+1/resize/680x453!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F63%2F7c%2F6f0487164079adcf022d2941e9b5%2Fvideo-team.jpg)

2020

Education Week celebrates a bold new look on edweek.org, realigning mission with brand. 2020 finds us with over 90 employees, an annual budget of $18 million and powerful offerings from Education Week, EdWeek Top School Jobs, EdWeek Market Brief. We continue to serve as the leading authority in education and are the comprehensive cornerstone for educators, policymakers, and business leaders alike. # Awards Announced for Outstanding Education Journalism in ’99

March 08, 2000  3 min read

*   [Print](javascript:window.print())

[Email](mailto:?body=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03%0A%0A%0AArticles%20on%20testing%2C%20desegregation%2C%20and%20early-childhood%20education%20are%20among%20the%20winners%20of%20the%201999%20National%20Awards%20for%20Education%20Reporting%2C%20announced%20last%20week%20by%20the%20Education%20Writers%20Association.)[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=200633758294132&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03)[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03&mini=true&title=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999&summary=%0AArticles%20on%20testing%2C%20desegregation%2C%20and%20early-childhood%20education%20are%20among%20the%20winners%20of%20the%201999%20National%20Awards%20for%20Education%20Reporting%2C%20announced%20last%20week%20by%20the%20Education%20Writers%20Association.&source=Education%20Week)[Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.edweek.org%2Feducation%2Fawards-announced-for-outstanding-education-journalism-in-99%2F2000%2F03&text=Awards%20Announced%20for%20Outstanding%20Education%20Journalism%20in%20%E2%80%9999)Copy URL

Articles on testing, desegregation, and early-childhood education are among the winners of the 1999 National Awards for Education Reporting, announced last week by the Education Writers Association.

The awards, honoring coverage of education by print and broadcast journalists, were chosen from 459 entries and were selected by a panel of reporters, editors, college professors, and educators.

First-place winners will receive $250 and a plaque. Second-place winners will receive a certificate.

An overall award chosen from among the winners, the Fred M. Hechinger Grand Prize for Distinguished Education Reporting, will be presented at the EWA’s annual convention in Atlanta next month.

_Education Week_ received a special citation in the special interest/trade publication category, to which the newspaper is assigned, for its yearlong series about the development of public education over the past 100 years, _Lessons of a Century_. The winning entry in that category was an article, [“Generation of Cheaters,”](http://www.asbj.com/199904/0499coverstory.html) by Kevin Bushweller, in the _American School Board Journal._

Other first-place winners are:

**Newspapers over 100,000 circulation:**

Breaking news: “Deciding Desegregation,” by Celeste Smith, Debbie Cenziper, Jennifer Wing Rothacker, and Ted Mellnik, _The Charlotte_ (N.C.) _Observer_.

**Features:** “A Life’s Lesson,” by Chris Moran, _The San Diego Union-Tribune._

**News feature or issue package:** “Educating Alex,” by John Gittelsohn and Bruce Chambers, _The Orange County_ (Calif.) _Register_.

**Series or group of articles:** “Worlds Apart,” by Tim Simmons, _The News & Observer_, Raleigh, N.C.

**Investigative reporting:** “Dirty Secrets,” by Jane Elizabeth Zemel and Steve Twedt, the _Pittsburgh Post-Gazette._

**Opinion:** “Early Childhood Well-Being,” by Linda Valdez, _The Arizona Republic_, Phoenix.

**Special section or page:** “3 to 6: The Teen Alone Zone,” by Kate Taylor, Lisa Daniels, Robin Franzen, Gillian Gaynair, Spencer Heinz, Romel Hernandez, Inara Verzemnieks, Chris Broderick, and Susan Gage, _The Oregonian_, Portland.

**Newspapers under 100,000 circulation:**

Breaking news: “A War Over Words,” by Jennifer Rose Marino, the _Savannah_ (Ga.) _Morning News_.

**Features:** “No Way Out,” by Kathryn C. Eastburn, _Colorado Springs_ (Colo.) _Independent_.

**News feature or issue package:** “None of the Above,” by Nigel Jaquiss _, Willamette Week_, Portland, Ore.

**Series or group of articles:** “Reinventing Our Public Schools,” by Marjorie Coeyman, Stephanie Cook, Mark Clayton, and Gail Russell Chaddock, _The Christian Science Monitor._

**Investigative reporting (tie):** “A System Padded With Patronage,” by Sean Patrick Lyons and staff, _Waterbury_ (Conn.) _Republican-American_; and “Investigation of University of Colorado President,” by Brian Hansen, Pamela White, Terje Langeland, Mark Collins, and Amanda Hill, _Colorado Daily_, University of Colorado at Boulder.

**Opinion:** “Rx for taas,” by John P. Young, _Waco_ (Texas) _Tribune-Herald_.

**Special section or page:** “Heralding the New Millennium,” by Carol Trapani, Kathleen Norton, Dolores Pinto, John A. Torres, Michelle Vellucci, and others, _Poughkeepsie_ (N.Y.) _Journal_.

**Magazines**

National magazine article: “Schooling the Imagination,” by Todd Oppenheimer, _The_ _Atlantic Monthly_.

**Regional/local magazine article:** “Hitting the Books,” by Jennifer O’Donnell, _Tidewater Parent_, Virginia Beach, Va.

**Broadcast**

Hard news and investigative coverage, television: “Teacher Shortage: False Alarm?,” by John Merrow, John D. Tulenko, Ivan Crowther, and Merill Stern, “The Merrow Report,” PBS.

**Documentary and feature, TV:** “Secrets of the SAT,” by Michael Chandler and Sharon Tiller, WGBH Frontline West, Berkeley, Calif.

**Radio:** “Education Reform,” by Kathryn Baron, KQED-FM, San Francisco.

**—Alan Richard**

## Our Leaders

*   ## Michele J. Givens

President and CEO

Michele Givens is an experienced and strategically focused publishing executive who has helped lead the nonprofit media organization, best known for publishing Education Week, in a time of profound and often difficult change.

She joined EPE as general manager in 2001 and formally received the concurrent title of publisher in 2009. In June 2016, the EPE Board of Trustees announced her appointment to succeed her longtime colleague Virginia B. Edwards as the organization’s president and CEO, effective August 1, 2016.

Previously in her career, Givens was the consumer marketing director for Outside magazine in Santa Fe, N.M.; associate consumer marketing manager at Rodale Press in Emmaus, Pa.; and circulation director at McGraw-Hill in Washington, D.C.

Givens earned an M.S. in the Management of Information Technology from the University of Virginia, an M.B.A. from the University of New Mexico, and a bachelor’s degree from George Mason University.

She serves on the board of directors of the Center for Teaching Quality and is a member of the National Press Club.  ![Image 3: Michele Givens](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b837ba/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3164x4768+0+0/resize/215x324!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F07%2Ffb%2Fb7e8ac66477c93e0a1cd139aef68%2Fmichele-givens-2-jb.jpg)

## Beth Frerking

Editor-in-Chief

Beth Frerking, a veteran journalist and newsroom leader who has worked as a top editor, reporter, and journalism educator, currently serves as editor-in-chief for Education Week.

Frerking’s achievements include being named a magazine innovator by the [Folio: 100 Awards](https://archive.foliomag.com/events/folio-100-awards-networking-reception-2017/) and two National Headliner awards for her work covering children, families, and education. While at The Dallas Times Herald,she was part of a reporting team that covered the crash of Delta Flight 191. This work was a finalist for the [Pulitzer Prize in Public Service](https://www.pulitzer.org/finalists/staff-28).

Her other accomplishments include helping to launch and oversee the Education Lab, a community-funded reporting team created to expand in-depth education coverage at The Dallas Morning News, and helping to establish The Politico Network, a content-sharing network that included more than 100 news organizations, two-thirds of which were newspapers.

Frerking’s previous experience includes editor-in-chief of The National Law Journal;senior editor and assistant managing editor at Politico; news vertical editor at The Dallas Morning News; national correspondent for the former Newhouse News Service; Washington bureau chief and congressional correspondent for The Denver Post; director of the Journalism Center on Children & Families, previously part of the Philip Merrill College of Journalism at the University of Maryland, and editor of The Daily Texan.

Frerking is an honors graduate of University of Texas at Austin’s School of Journalism.       ![Image 4: Beth Frerking](https://epe.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/371f09b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3354x5054+15+0/resize/215x324!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fepe-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fc7%2Fdb%2F094a12a348fa9a3e8f8f40b5bb9b%2Fbeth-frerking-jb.jpg)

# Student Support Services

At the Intergenerational Schools, we’re committed to supporting the whole child: academically, socially, and emotionally. Every student has unique strengths and needs, and we provide a range of services, programs, and resources to ensure each student receives the support they need to thrive.

Our approach includes in-school counseling, intervention specialists, special education services, and connections to community-based resources. We also help families access scholarship programs, meal assistance, and college credit opportunities that can reduce barriers and expand possibilities for students.

Below, you’ll find information about the support services available to students and families at the Intergenerational Schools.

[Scholarships](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#scholarships)

[Free Meals](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#meals)

[Summer EBT](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#sun-bucks)

[Transportation](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#transportation)

## Scholarships and Credits

#### College Credit Plus

Through a partnership with Cleveland State University, middle school students at the Intergenerational Schools can take college classes and earn college credits—completely free for families. This program is called College Credit Plus (CCP).

With CCP, students can take college courses while they’re still in middle school. They get support from both Cleveland State University and the Intergenerational Schools. This program helps students:

*   Get a head start on college
*   Save money on future college costs
*   Try out college-level work while still having their teachers’ support

[Learn More](link_29)

#### Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship

The Jon Peterson Special Needs (JPSN) Scholarship Program provides scholarships to students who are eligible to attend kindergarten through 12th grade and have an Individualized Education Program (IEP) from their district. The amount of each scholarship is based on the primary disability condition identified on the student’s Evaluation Team Report (ETR). Students must be enrolled in the scholarship program for the entire program year to receive the full scholarship amount.

[Visit the Ohio Department of Education’s website for more information about this resource.](link_30)

[Learn More](link_30)

#### Autism Scholarship Program

The Autism Scholarship Program (ASP) allows parents of eligible children with autism to choose a specialized education program outside their home school district. This program enables students to receive their education and access the services specified in their Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Autism Education Plan (AEP).

[Visit the Ohio Department of Education’s website for more information about this resource.](link_31)

[Learn More](link_31)

## Community Eligibility Program (CEP):  
Free Meals for Students

##### Good news! All students at the Intergenerational Schools get free breakfast and lunch every day.

Our schools qualify for a program called Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) under the National School Lunch Program and National School Breakfast Program. This means **every student can eat breakfast and lunch at school for free, without having to apply.**The CEP program reduces the burden for families and helps ensure students receive nutritious meals.

#### Important: We still need your help!

Even though meals are free, we need families to fill out a Household Income Form each year. This form is in your Welcome Packet or available at the front office.

**Why does this matter?**  
This form helps our schools get important funding from the state and federal government. Without it, we could lose money that pays for programs your child needs.

## Summer EBT (Sun Bucks)

##### Summer Grocery Help for Families

Does your child get free or reduced-price school meals? If yes, your family can get help buying groceries during the summer through a State of Ohio program called **Sun Bucks (also called Summer EBT).**

_(The Intergenerational Schools do not administer this program, determine eligibility or control the application timeline. [Please refer to the Ohio Department of Workforce & Education’s guide to Sun Bucks](link_33) for program details, FAQs, application and more.)_

#### Who can get Sun Bucks?

Children who qualify for free or reduced-price school meals automatically qualify for Sun Bucks.

#### How does it work?

Eligible families get $120 per child on an EBT card. You can use this card to buy food at participating stores during the summer when school meals aren’t available.

#### When will I get the money?

The Ohio Department of Education & Workforce runs this program. Check their website for updates on when payments will be sent out.

#### Do I need to apply?

Some families are automatically enrolled if their child gets free or reduced-price school meals. Other families may need to apply through their school district or the Ohio Department of Education & Workforce.

#### For more information:

Visit the Ohio Department of Education & Workforce website at [https://sebt.ohio.gov/](link_33).

## Transportation Information

##### Getting to School

The Intergenerational Schools do not provide or direct transportation for students, with some exceptions. However, to help our families navigate transportation options, we have a process to help determine students’ eligibility for bus transportation through Cleveland Metropolitan School District.

Under state law (Ohio Revised Code **§ 3327.01**), public school districts are responsible for providing transportation to students enrolled in community (charter) schools, provided certain conditions are met. This includes students residing in the**Cleveland Metropolitan School District (CMSD).**

##### Do you live in Cleveland?

If your child lives in Cleveland and goes to the Intergenerational Schools, Cleveland Metropolitan School District (CMSD) may provide bus service. Contact them to find out if your child qualifies:

##### CMSD Transportation Services

Phone: 216.838.4BUS (4287)

**Whether your child can get a bus depends on:**

*   What grade they’re in
*   How far you live from school

##### Important to know:

While we can help you apply for transportation, the Intergenerational Schools do not manage busing. Any questions about the following must go to CMSD Transportation:

*   Bus routes
*   Pick-up and drop-off times
*   Where the bus stops
*   Bus schedule changes
*   Bus delays

Please call CMSD Transportation 216.838.4BUS (4287) for information about these details.

#### Do you live outside Cleveland?

Contact your local school district’s transportation department. Ask if they provide transportation or payment help for students who attend charter schools.

#### Yellow Bus Application (2026-2027 School Year)

**Does your child qualify for a school bus?**

Fill out this application if your child meets these requirements:

*   Enrolled as a K-8th grade student at one of our schools for the 2025-2026 school year
*   Lives in the city of Cleveland
*   Lives more than 1 mile but less than 5 miles from school

Please note: Your child may not qualify for a bus if:

*   They don’t go to the closest Intergenerational School to your home
*   There is no bus route near your house

If your child doesn’t qualify for a bus, you may be able to get money to help pay for transportation instead.

**Important: You must fill out a separate application for each child.**

[Link to Yellow Bus Application](link_34)

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. These programs are led by teachers, parent volunteers, and community partners, and they change throughout the year based on student interest and available resources.

From creative arts and storytelling to cooking, gardening, journalism, and theater, clubs offer students a chance to discover what excites them in a supportive, multi-age environment. Recent clubs have included crochet, upcycling, health leadership, Girl Scouts, theater in partnership with Playhouse Square, cooking through Food Strong, and student journalism. Each campus offers different programs each quarter, so check Bloomz for current offerings and sign-up information.

## Overview of Model Middle School

Model Middle School is a public school located in Rome, GA, which is in a fringe rural setting. The student population of Model Middle School is 550 and the school serves 5-7. At Model Middle School, 52% of students scored at or above the proficient level for math, and 52% scored at or above that level for reading.The student-teacher ratio is 14:1, which is the same as that of the district.The student population is made up of 46% female students and 54% male students. The school enrolls 43% economically disadvantaged students. There are 38 equivalent full-time teachers.

# Near West Intergenerational School

#### Ohio City, Cleveland

Welcome to Near West Intergenerational School, where students learn at their own pace in small, multi-age classes. Here, every child is known, valued, and encouraged to grow as a confident, curious learner.

#### About Our Campus

## A Vibrant Community in Ohio City

Near West Intergenerational School opened in 2011 in Cleveland’s Ohio City neighborhood as the first charter-district partnership in the State of Ohio to co-locate with a district school in the same building (as part of the Cleveland Plan). For over a decade, Near West has served families from Ohio City, surrounding west-side neighborhoods, building a vibrant learning community rooted in collaboration, creativity, and connection.

Our students benefit from strong partnerships with nearby senior centers and community organizations, and a school culture that celebrates both individual growth and shared success. In our classrooms, students of different ages and abilities learn together, supporting each other’s development and building relationships that strengthen the entire school community.

Near West has consistently demonstrated academic excellence, earning the Ohio Community School of Quality designation every year since 2019, and most recently 4.5 stars on the Ohio School Report Card for two consecutive years. and ranking #3 overall out of 107 K-8 public schools in Cleveland.

This recognition reflects the dedication of our staff, families, and volunteers who work together to create a joyful, supportive environment where every student can thrive.

#### Our Campus at a Glance

## Quick Facts

Near West Intergenerational School opened in 2011 in Cleveland’s Ohio City neighborhood, serving families from across the west side. With a 4.5-star rating on the Ohio School Report Card for two consecutive years, Near West has built a strong reputation for academic excellence and a warm, welcoming community where students of all ages learn and grow together.

## Not sure which campus is right for you?

Both campuses offer the same high-quality education and follow the same developmental model. Most families choose based on proximity to home. Contact us if you’d like to schedule tours at both schools or have questions about enrollment.

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. These programs are led by teachers, parent volunteers, and community partners, and they change throughout the year based on student interest and available resources.

From creative arts and storytelling to cooking, gardening, journalism, and theater, clubs offer students a chance to discover what excites them in a supportive, multi-age environment. Recent clubs have included crochet, upcycling, health leadership, Girl Scouts, theater in partnership with Playhouse Square, cooking through Food Strong, and student journalism. Each campus offers different programs each quarter, so check Bloomz for current offerings and sign-up information.

#### On-Site After-School Care at TIS-East

The Intergenerational School – East partners with the Boys & Girls Club of Northeast Ohio to provide on-site after-school care. Families interested in this program should enroll directly through the Boys & Girls Club.

# Innovating Education: 25 Years of Doing School Differently

by [Brooke King, CEO](https://igschools.org/author/alexbrandpivotinc-com/ "Posts by Brooke King, CEO") | Mar 30, 2026 | [News](https://igschools.org/category/news/) | [0 comments](https://igschools.org/innovating-education-25-years-of-doing-school-differently/#respond)

![Image 3](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Lifelong-Learners-March-2026-featured-image-1080x675.png)

Innovation means building around what works, not just what’s new. For 25 years, the Intergenerational Schools have designed every element of our model around two core truths: children learn at different paces and in different ways, and community strengthens learning across generations.

This quarter, we have good reason to reflect on what that commitment looks like over time. The Intergenerational Schools have been named a 2025 Program of Distinction by Generations United — a national recognition of outstanding intergenerational programs — and you can read more about that designation in our [spring 2026 newsletter.](https://canva.link/st6vwy174pvn6so)

This year also brought another milestone:A chapter I authored on the Intergenerational Schools appears in the newly published [Oxford Handbook of Intergenerational Connection](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/60669?login=false) (Oxford University Press, 2025).The chapter traces the reasons our model was built with intergenerational programs at its center, how those programs have grown and navigated real challenges including the pandemic, and how we continue to deepen community engagement today.

These are both examples of the Intergenerational Schools’ commitment to seeing school differently. Every day, our teachers, staff, students and families work together to innovate education. This commitment fosters a model that keeps working because it was built around what children and communities actually need. Thank you for being part of it.

Brooke King, CEO  
 Intergenerational Schools

_Explore our [spring 2026 newsletter](https://canva.link/st6vwy174pvn6so) for stories about innovating education at the Intergenerational Schools._

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. These programs are led by teachers, parent volunteers, and community partners, and they change throughout the year based on student interest and available resources.

From creative arts and storytelling to cooking, gardening, journalism, and theater, clubs offer students a chance to discover what excites them in a supportive, multi-age environment. Recent clubs have included crochet, upcycling, health leadership, Girl Scouts, theater in partnership with Playhouse Square, cooking through Food Strong, and student journalism. Each campus offers different programs each quarter, so check Bloomz for current offerings and sign-up information.

#### On-Site After-School Care at TIS-East

The Intergenerational School – East partners with the Boys & Girls Club of Northeast Ohio to provide on-site after-school care. Families interested in this program should enroll directly through the Boys & Girls Club.

#### Transportation to Off-Site Childcare

Both campuses provide bus transportation to participating childcare centers near each school. Current participating centers include:

**Near West:**

*   Horizon Education Centers
*   Tiny Footsteps Child Enrichment Center

# Impact & Innovation

For 25 years, the Intergenerational Schools have been proving that education works best when it’s built around relationships, individualized learning, and community connection. Our multi-age classrooms, developmental curriculum, and intergenerational partnerships create an environment where students don’t just prepare for tests, they develop the confidence, curiosity, and critical thinking skills that lead to long-term success.

Our track record speaks for itself. Students at both campuses consistently outperform peers at nearby schools on state assessments. Our model has been recognized nationally and studied by researchers at Case Western Reserve University and other institutions. And our graduates go on to Northeast Ohio’s top high schools, prepared not just academically but with the social-emotional skills to thrive. Below, you’ll find annual reports and school performance data that demonstrate the strength and sustainability of our approach.

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. These programs are led by teachers, parent volunteers, and community partners, and they change throughout the year based on student interest and available resources.

From creative arts and storytelling to cooking, gardening, journalism, and theater, clubs offer students a chance to discover what excites them in a supportive, multi-age environment. Recent clubs have included crochet, upcycling, health leadership, Girl Scouts, theater in partnership with Playhouse Square, cooking through Food Strong, and student journalism. Each campus offers different programs each quarter, so check Bloomz for current offerings and sign-up information.

#### On-Site After-School Care at TIS-East

The Intergenerational School – East partners with the Boys & Girls Club of Northeast Ohio to provide on-site after-school care. Families interested in this program should enroll directly through the Boys & Girls Club.

## Overview

Massachusetts Institute of Technology is a private institution that was founded in 1861. In the 2027 edition of Best Colleges, Massachusetts Institute of Technology is ranked No. 1 in National Universities.

It has a total undergraduate enrollment of 4,561 (fall 2025), its setting is city, and the campus size is 168 acres. The student-faculty ratio at Massachusetts Institute of Technology is 8:1, and it utilizes a 4-1-4-based academic calendar.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology does not accept the Common Application. The school's tuition and fees are $67,140. Fifty-eight percent of first-year students receive need-based financial aid, and the average net price for federal loan recipients is $20,338.

The four-year graduation rate is 86%. Six years after graduation, the median salary for graduates is $131,633.

# Community Partnerships

### Growing Community Through Collaboration

Across Cleveland, we’re building partnerships that strengthen both our schools and the broader community. Our partners help students apply what they learn in class, explore new interests, develop civic leadership, and understand their role in the world beyond school.

These partnerships take many forms: weekly or monthly intergenerational visits at senior centers and care facilities, community-based services provided on-site at our schools, group volunteer activities for corporate and service organizations, fundraising events hosted by local businesses, and collaborative programs that bring new resources and experiences into our classrooms. Each partnership is built on shared values and a commitment to meaningful engagement that benefits everyone involved.

If your organization is interested in partnering with the Intergenerational Schools, we’d love to hear from you. [Contact us](https://igschools.org/partnerships/#contact) below to explore how we can work together.

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. These programs are led by teachers, parent volunteers, and community partners, and they change throughout the year based on student interest and available resources.

From creative arts and storytelling to cooking, gardening, journalism, and theater, clubs offer students a chance to discover what excites them in a supportive, multi-age environment. Recent clubs have included crochet, upcycling, health leadership, Girl Scouts, theater in partnership with Playhouse Square, cooking through Food Strong, and student journalism. Each campus offers different programs each quarter, so check Bloomz for current offerings and sign-up information.

#### On-Site After-School Care at TIS-East

The Intergenerational School – East partners with the Boys & Girls Club of Northeast Ohio to provide on-site after-school care. Families interested in this program should enroll directly through the Boys & Girls Club.

#### Transportation to Off-Site Childcare

Both campuses provide bus transportation to participating childcare centers near each school. Current participating centers include:

**Near West:**

*   Horizon Education Centers
*   Tiny Footsteps Child Enrichment Center

**TIS-East:**

*   East End Neighborhood House
*   Fundamentals Academy
*   The Meeting Place

# Why We Exist

## Our Mission

The Intergenerational Schools connect, create, and guide a multi-generational community of lifelong learners and spirited citizens as they strive for academic excellence. 

![Image 3](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Group-227@2x.png)

## Our Vision

The Intergenerational Schools are a top choice in public education for Greater Cleveland families. We foster joyful and independent academic and social-emotional learning that allows students and learners of all ages to excel both individually and together in one equitable community. As innovative and progressive educators, we are catalysts and collaborators in improving public education that transforms Cleveland.

These aren’t just words on a page. Our mission and vision guide every decision we make, from how we structure our multi-age classrooms to how we partner with senior centers and community organizations. We believe learning happens best in community, where every person—regardless of age—has something to teach and something to learn. This approach creates an educational experience where students don’t just prepare for the future; they actively contribute to their communities today.

## Our Story

The first Intergenerational School opened in 2000, founded by child psychologist turned educator Catherine C. Whitehouse, Ph.D.; neurologist/gerontologist Peter J. Whitehouse, M.D., Ph.D.; and Stephanie FallCreek, DSW, then executive director at Fairhill Partners. They shared a belief that learning is a lifelong pursuit and that breaking down age barriers could transform education for children and enrich the lives of older adults. The school welcomed its first students as a free public charter school, offering Cleveland families an innovative alternative where older adults partnered with students to foster curiosity, share wisdom, and build meaningful relationships across generations.

By 2010, the school served over 200 students in kindergarten through eighth grade and had earned recognition locally and nationally for its effective model. In 2011, Near West Intergenerational School opened in the Ohio City neighborhood in response to demand from west-side families. This campus became the first charter-district partnership in the State of Ohio to co-locate a charter and district school in the same building—a milestone in collaborative public education, and an important part of the newly legislated Cleveland Plan.

Today, the Intergenerational Schools serve approximately 450 students across two campuses: The Intergenerational School–East in the Buckeye neighborhood and Near West Intergenerational School in Ohio City. Both schools have earned recognition as Community Schools of Quality by the Ohio Department of Education, and Near West consistently ranks among the top 3 K-8 public schools in Cleveland.

In 2014, the network received the national Eisner Prize for Lifetime Achievement in Intergenerational Excellence. These awards reflect years of dedicated work by our staff, families, volunteers, and community partners who believe in the power of intergenerational learning.

## 25 Years.

## Countless Moments.

For 25 years, the Intergenerational Schools have been creating countless moments of connection, growth, and discovery across Cleveland. From our founding in 2000 to today, we’ve remained committed to building community and fostering lifelong learning for students, families, and volunteers of all ages. Help us celebrate by sharing your favorite memory. Send an email to [advancement@igschools.org.](mailto:advancement@igschools.org)

[Share Your Moment](mailto:advancement@igschools.org)

## Where We’re Going

Our work continues. While we’re proud of what we’ve built over 25 years, we remain focused on closing achievement gaps, expanding access to joyful learning, and proving that a different kind of public education is possible. We’re committed to supporting every student as they discover their strengths, build resilience, and learn what it means to be a spirited citizen. The community of students, families, staff, volunteers, and partners that we’ve grown together makes this work possible, and we’re grateful to everyone who walks this path with us.

# The Intergenerational School–East

#### Buckeye-Woodhill, Cleveland

Welcome to The Intergenerational School – East, the founding campus of the Intergenerational Schools network. For 25 years, TIS–East has been proving that learning is stronger when students, families, and community members of all ages come together. Here, every child is known, valued, and encouraged to grow as a confident, curious learner.

#### About Our Campus

## Where it All Began

The Intergenerational School – East is the flagship campus of the Intergenerational Schools network, opening in 2000 with a vision of breaking down age barriers and creating meaningful connections across generations. Located in Cleveland’s Buckeye-Woodhill neighborhood, TIS–East has spent 25 years demonstrating what’s possible when education centers on relationships, individualized learning, and community.

Our students engage in hands-on learning, student-led projects, and partnerships with organizations like Case Western Reserve University and local senior centers. From leading Earth Day Fairs to presenting research at university symposiums, TIS–East students build confidence through real-world experiences that extend far beyond the classroom.

The school serves families from across Cleveland’s east side, creating a diverse learning community where students of different ages, backgrounds, and experiences learn together in small, supportive classrooms. Our teachers stay with students for multiple years, building deep relationships that help every child reach their potential.

TIS–East has made significant academic progress, improving its overall rating on the Ohio School Report Card and jumping from 1 to 3 stars in Gap Closing, a measure of how well schools support all students. The campus also dramatically reduced chronic absenteeism, proof that students feel connected, engaged, and eager to be here.

![Image 3: TIS-Stay-in-the-Game-2025](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/544759584_758257633585443_8489821897019922451_n.jpg)

![Image 4: tmp_5eb229dd-6e49-48dc-9ce1-35fc27963daa](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/tmp_5eb229dd-6e49-48dc-9ce1-35fc27963daa.png)

![Image 5: 539497046_750283521049521_6782123285214839097_n](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/20250411_133021-scaled.jpg)

#### Meet Our Principal

## Aziz Ahmad

Principal, The Intergenerational School–East

“Welcome to TIS–East! I’m honored to lead the founding campus of the Intergenerational Schools, and I’m excited about where we’re headed. This school has always been a place where students are encouraged to be themselves, take risks, and discover what they’re capable of. That spirit continues today.

What I love most about TIS–East is the sense of community. Our students, families, staff, and partners all work together to create a school where everyone belongs. We celebrate growth in all its forms, whether it’s a student mastering a new skill, showing up consistently, or finding the courage to share their voice. Every step forward matters.

Our students are capable of incredible things, and my job is to make sure they know it. I’m committed to building on the strong foundation of this school and continuing to push for even greater success. My dream is for TIS–East to become the first 5-star K-8 school in Cleveland, and I believe that together, we can do it.

I look forward to meeting you and your family. Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions or would like to schedule a tour.”

#### Our Campus at a Glance

## Quick Facts

The Intergenerational School – East is the founding campus of the Intergenerational Schools network, opening in 2000. For 25 years, TIS–East has served families from across Cleveland’s east side, building a diverse learning community rooted in relationships, hands-on learning, and meaningful connections across generations.

Clubs and activities offered by staff throughout the year. Families can also sign up with the Boys & Girls Club of Northeast Ohio for their onsite after-care program.

## Not sure which campus is right for you?

Both campuses offer the same high-quality education and follow the same developmental model. Most families choose based on proximity to home. Contact us if you’d like to schedule tours at both schools or have questions about enrollment.

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. ## Overview

Massachusetts Institute of Technology is a private institution that was founded in 1861. In the 2027 edition of Best Colleges, Massachusetts Institute of Technology is ranked No. 1 in National Universities.

It has a total undergraduate enrollment of 4,561 (fall 2025), its setting is city, and the campus size is 168 acres. The student-faculty ratio at Massachusetts Institute of Technology is 8:1, and it utilizes a 4-1-4-based academic calendar.

Massachusetts Institute of Technology does not accept the Common Application. The school's tuition and fees are $67,140. Fifty-eight percent of first-year students receive need-based financial aid, and the average net price for federal loan recipients is $20,338.

The four-year graduation rate is 86%. Six years after graduation, the median salary for graduates is $131,633.

### Attended 20 years ago, would repeat

If you're an engineer or scientist at heart, you can't go wrong with MIT. People think of a liberal arts education as rounding out a person and teaching them analytical skills. MIT does that in the sciences and engineering. Other reviewers already talk about the MIT experience so as an old timer, I'll mostly talk about life after the 'Tute. Education: MIT definitely gave me a solid foundation upon which to learn other topics. You can never learn enough in four years to last a lifetime, but the foundation I received made other and newer topics easily accessible. Reputation: automatic assumption of intelligence, hard work, and credibility in the work place. That reputation is well deserved. What you lack from formal education, you pick up after MIT through independent continued education. What MIT taught me was how to solve problems because what is engineering but solving problems using foundational sciences. Acceptance: people accepted each other completely with little to no judgment. We can be kooky or silly and it was appreciated. I think that's why many alums appreciated being able to be their genuine selves during their time at MIT, something that's lost in the "real world". After MIT, that experience of being your genuine selves may raise eyebrows in your 20's, but it's what most of us settle on by our 50's or 60's. So you just shortcut your maturation. (Btw, there is a workplace balance) Support: my faculty advisor was incredible and we stayed in touch long after. I think that was the gem at MIT. Network: MIT does very well, but this is the one thing that I think Harvard (where I also attended) and maybe a couple other Ivys do better. The MIT alumni network is strong and I'd give it an A-. From personal experience, I found the Harvard one the gold standard. Overall: I was admitted to other schools. In my graduate years, I had the opportunity to study elsewhere and somewhat (imperfectly) compare the various schools. I'd happily choose MIT again.

# The Intergenerational School–East

#### Buckeye-Woodhill, Cleveland

Welcome to The Intergenerational School – East, the founding campus of the Intergenerational Schools network. For 25 years, TIS–East has been proving that learning is stronger when students, families, and community members of all ages come together. Here, every child is known, valued, and encouraged to grow as a confident, curious learner.

#### About Our Campus

## Where it All Began

The Intergenerational School – East is the flagship campus of the Intergenerational Schools network, opening in 2000 with a vision of breaking down age barriers and creating meaningful connections across generations. Located in Cleveland’s Buckeye-Woodhill neighborhood, TIS–East has spent 25 years demonstrating what’s possible when education centers on relationships, individualized learning, and community.

Our students engage in hands-on learning, student-led projects, and partnerships with organizations like Case Western Reserve University and local senior centers. From leading Earth Day Fairs to presenting research at university symposiums, TIS–East students build confidence through real-world experiences that extend far beyond the classroom.

The school serves families from across Cleveland’s east side, creating a diverse learning community where students of different ages, backgrounds, and experiences learn together in small, supportive classrooms. Our teachers stay with students for multiple years, building deep relationships that help every child reach their potential.

TIS–East has made significant academic progress, improving its overall rating on the Ohio School Report Card and jumping from 1 to 3 stars in Gap Closing, a measure of how well schools support all students. The campus also dramatically reduced chronic absenteeism, proof that students feel connected, engaged, and eager to be here.

#### Meet Our Principal

## Aziz Ahmad

Principal, The Intergenerational School–East

“Welcome to TIS–East! I’m honored to lead the founding campus of the Intergenerational Schools, and I’m excited about where we’re headed. This school has always been a place where students are encouraged to be themselves, take risks, and discover what they’re capable of. That spirit continues today.

What I love most about TIS–East is the sense of community. Our students, families, staff, and partners all work together to create a school where everyone belongs. We celebrate growth in all its forms, whether it’s a student mastering a new skill, showing up consistently, or finding the courage to share their voice. Every step forward matters.

Our students are capable of incredible things, and my job is to make sure they know it. I’m committed to building on the strong foundation of this school and continuing to push for even greater success. My dream is for TIS–East to become the first 5-star K-8 school in Cleveland, and I believe that together, we can do it.

I look forward to meeting you and your family. Please don’t hesitate to reach out if you have questions or would like to schedule a tour.”

## Sports, Clubs & After School

Beyond the school day, students at the Intergenerational Schools have opportunities to explore their interests, build new skills, and connect with peers through a variety of after-school clubs and activities. # Student Support Services

At the Intergenerational Schools, we’re committed to supporting the whole child: academically, socially, and emotionally. Every student has unique strengths and needs, and we provide a range of services, programs, and resources to ensure each student receives the support they need to thrive.

Our approach includes in-school counseling, intervention specialists, special education services, and connections to community-based resources. We also help families access scholarship programs, meal assistance, and college credit opportunities that can reduce barriers and expand possibilities for students.

Below, you’ll find information about the support services available to students and families at the Intergenerational Schools.

[Scholarships](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#scholarships)

[Free Meals](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#meals)

[Summer EBT](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#sun-bucks)

[Transportation](https://igschools.org/family-portal/student-support-services/#transportation)

## Scholarships and Credits

#### College Credit Plus

Through a partnership with Cleveland State University, middle school students at the Intergenerational Schools can take college classes and earn college credits—completely free for families. This program is called College Credit Plus (CCP).

With CCP, students can take college courses while they’re still in middle school. They get support from both Cleveland State University and the Intergenerational Schools. This program helps students:

*   Get a head start on college
*   Save money on future college costs
*   Try out college-level work while still having their teachers’ support

[Learn More](https://igschools.org/ccp-information/)

#### Jon Peterson Special Needs Scholarship

The Jon Peterson Special Needs (JPSN) Scholarship Program provides scholarships to students who are eligible to attend kindergarten through 12th grade and have an Individualized Education Program (IEP) from their district. The amount of each scholarship is based on the primary disability condition identified on the student’s Evaluation Team Report (ETR). Students must be enrolled in the scholarship program for the entire program year to receive the full scholarship amount.

[Visit the Ohio Department of Education’s website for more information about this resource.](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Other-Resources/Scholarships/Jon-Peterson-Special-Needs-Scholarship)

[Learn More](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Other-Resources/Scholarships/Jon-Peterson-Special-Needs-Scholarship)

#### Autism Scholarship Program

The Autism Scholarship Program (ASP) allows parents of eligible children with autism to choose a specialized education program outside their home school district. This program enables students to receive their education and access the services specified in their Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Autism Education Plan (AEP).

[Visit the Ohio Department of Education’s website for more information about this resource.](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Other-Resources/Scholarships/Autism-Scholarship)

[Learn More](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Other-Resources/Scholarships/Autism-Scholarship)

## Community Eligibility Program (CEP):  
Free Meals for Students

##### Good news! All students at the Intergenerational Schools get free breakfast and lunch every day.

Our schools qualify for a program called Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) under the National School Lunch Program and National School Breakfast Program. This means **every student can eat breakfast and lunch at school for free, without having to apply.**The CEP program reduces the burden for families and helps ensure students receive nutritious meals.

## Summer EBT (Sun Bucks)

##### Summer Grocery Help for Families

Does your child get free or reduced-price school meals? If yes, your family can get help buying groceries during the summer through a State of Ohio program called **Sun Bucks (also called Summer EBT).**

_(The Intergenerational Schools do not administer this program, determine eligibility or control the application timeline. [Please refer to the Ohio Department of Workforce & Education’s guide to Sun Bucks](https://sebt.ohio.gov/) for program details, FAQs, application and more.)_

#### Who can get Sun Bucks?

Children who qualify for free or reduced-price school meals automatically qualify for Sun Bucks.

#### How does it work?

Eligible families get $120 per child on an EBT card. You can use this card to buy food at participating stores during the summer when school meals aren’t available.

#### When will I get the money?

The Ohio Department of Education & Workforce runs this program. Check their website for updates on when payments will be sent out.

#### Do I need to apply?

Some families are automatically enrolled if their child gets free or reduced-price school meals. Other families may need to apply through their school district or the Ohio Department of Education & Workforce.

#### For more information:

Visit the Ohio Department of Education & Workforce website at [https://sebt.ohio.gov/](https://sebt.ohio.gov/).

## Transportation Information

##### Getting to School

The Intergenerational Schools do not provide or direct transportation for students, with some exceptions. However, to help our families navigate transportation options, we have a process to help determine students’ eligibility for bus transportation through Cleveland Metropolitan School District.

Under state law (Ohio Revised Code **§ 3327.01**), public school districts are responsible for providing transportation to students enrolled in community (charter) schools, provided certain conditions are met. This includes students residing in the**Cleveland Metropolitan School District (CMSD).**

##### Do you live in Cleveland?

If your child lives in Cleveland and goes to the Intergenerational Schools, Cleveland Metropolitan School District (CMSD) may provide bus service. Contact them to find out if your child qualifies:

##### CMSD Transportation Services

Phone: 216.838.4BUS (4287)

**Whether your child can get a bus depends on:**

*   What grade they’re in
*   How far you live from school

##### Important to know:

While we can help you apply for transportation, the Intergenerational Schools do not manage busing. Any questions about the following must go to CMSD Transportation:

*   Bus routes
*   Pick-up and drop-off times
*   Where the bus stops
*   Bus schedule changes
*   Bus delays

Please call CMSD Transportation 216.838.4BUS (4287) for information about these details.

#### Do you live outside Cleveland?

Contact your local school district’s transportation department. Ask if they provide transportation or payment help for students who attend charter schools.

#### Yellow Bus Application (2026-2027 School Year)

**Does your child qualify for a school bus?**

Fill out this application if your child meets these requirements:

*   Enrolled as a K-8th grade student at one of our schools for the 2025-2026 school year
*   Lives in the city of Cleveland
*   Lives more than 1 mile but less than 5 miles from school

Please note: Your child may not qualify for a bus if:

*   They don’t go to the closest Intergenerational School to your home
*   There is no bus route near your house

If your child doesn’t qualify for a bus, you may be able to get money to help pay for transportation instead.

**Important: You must fill out a separate application for each child.**

[Link to Yellow Bus Application](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdYXyO8-Wh6VCgDJDutjz2f8dUB2VeUbZWjq_zqx7C1ozPHjA/viewform)

# Community Partnerships

### Growing Community Through Collaboration

Across Cleveland, we’re building partnerships that strengthen both our schools and the broader community. Our partners help students apply what they learn in class, explore new interests, develop civic leadership, and understand their role in the world beyond school.

These partnerships take many forms: weekly or monthly intergenerational visits at senior centers and care facilities, community-based services provided on-site at our schools, group volunteer activities for corporate and service organizations, fundraising events hosted by local businesses, and collaborative programs that bring new resources and experiences into our classrooms. Each partnership is built on shared values and a commitment to meaningful engagement that benefits everyone involved.

If your organization is interested in partnering with the Intergenerational Schools, we’d love to hear from you. [Contact us](https://igschools.org/partnerships/#contact) below to explore how we can work together.

## Our Partners

![Image 6](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/1tzdaxHaXZmjYKLA-BGCNEO-Logo_Original-scaled-e1772212943590.png)

## Boys & Girls Clubs of Northeast Ohio

Our collaboration with Boys & Girsl Clubs of NEO at TIS-East extends learning beyond the school day in a safe, structured environment that reinforces academic growth, leadership development, and positive community relationships.

![Image 7](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/case_western_reserve-university-logo-freelogovectors.net_-e1772212931343.png)

## Case Western Reserve University

We partner with Case Western Reserve University each year on Earth Day projects at these university-hosted events, demonstrating informed climate action and the strength of intergenerational learning in addressing environmental challenges. The partnership also includes leadership development through administrative retreats at Sears thinkbox, supporting innovation and strategic growth across our schools.

![Image 8](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/cmsdlogostacked-rgb.webp)

## Cleveland Metropolitan School District

CMSD serves as the charter sponsor for our schools. Through this sponsorship, CMSD provides oversight, accountability, and strategic support to ensure strong academic performance, governance, and operational integrity. This partnership reinforces a shared commitment to expanding high-quality public school options for Cleveland families while maintaining rigorous standards and student-centered outcomes.

![Image 9](https://igschools.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Edwins-e1772212957430.png)

## Sports, Clubs & After School

# Impact & Innovation

For 25 years, the Intergenerational Schools have been proving that education works best when it’s built around relationships, individualized learning, and community connection. Our multi-age classrooms, developmental curriculum, and intergenerational partnerships create an environment where students don’t just prepare for tests, they develop the confidence, curiosity, and critical thinking skills that lead to long-term success.

Our track record speaks for itself. Students at both campuses consistently outperform peers at nearby schools on state assessments. Our model has been recognized nationally and studied by researchers at Case Western Reserve University and other institutions. And our graduates go on to Northeast Ohio’s top high schools, prepared not just academically but with the social-emotional skills to thrive. Below, you’ll find annual reports and school performance data that demonstrate the strength and sustainability of our approach.

## AGENDA 

I. Call to Order 

II. Agenda Changes / Table File 

III. Public Comment 

This is aa opportunity for members of the school district to address the Board. You are requested to do so from the podium. After being recognized by the chair, each individual will identify himself/herself and the group represented, if any. He/She will then state the reason for addressing the Board. To insure that all individuals have a chance to speak, speakers will be limited to one three-minute presentation. Please know that this is not a time to debate an issue, but for you to make your comments.

Explanation o f Agenda Items for the January 13, 2014, School Board M eeting 

Call to Order 

Agenda Changes / Table File Public Comment Approval of Minutes 

Minutes of die Regular School Board meeting held on December 9, 2013, are enclosed for your review and comment. 

Announcements and Recognitions Items for Discussion and / or Reports 

1. Prairie Creek Community School and Arcadia Charter School Annual Reports. 

Simon Tyler, Director o f Prairie Creek Community School, and Ryan Krorninga, Director of Arcadia, will be doing a joint presentation of the programs being provided in their two charter schools. 

Simon will be presenting a review of Prairie Creek's eleventii year of operation as a charter school under the sponsorship of the Northfield Public Schools, and an overview o f this current school year. Prairie Creek's 2012-2013 Annual Report is enclosed for your review. 

Ryan will review Arcadia’s program and present their 2012-2013 Annual Report, which is enclosed. 

Arcadia, formerly ARTech, is in its tenth year of operation. 

These reviews and written reports fulfill state requirements for annual reporting as well as our District’s request that each charter school authorized by the Northfield Public Schools present an annual report to the School Board. 

Superintendent's Report A. Items for Individual Action 

1. All Day Kindergarten Space in Elementary Buildings. 

The Superintendent’s Cabinet completed a thorough review o f the short-term need to provide a minimum of four full day kindergarten classrooms in each elementary building in order to support the implementation of state funded all day kindergarten in the Northfield Public Schools for the 2014-15 school year and beyond. The Board has reviewed the information and the recommended short-term option to support this implementation. They have had the opportunity to review the other options considered and understand the issues that resulted in the rejection of those options. 

Superintendent's Recommendation: Motion to approve providing space for four kindergarten classrooms at Sibley by relocating the District DCD Moderate program from Sibley Elementary to Greenvale Park Elementary beginning in the 2014-15 school year. 

2. Demographic Study. 

The Superintendent’s Cabinet has provided the Board with a significant amount o f information about the current demographics and building capacities of the District’s facilities. To develop a long-term plan to meet our student’s needs in the coming years, we need projections of overall student enrollment for the next decade as well as well as a study o f district housing, neighborhoods and demographics that will allow us to predict the District’s future population and facilities needs. School Board Memorandum January 13, 2014 Page Two 

Superintendent's Recommendation: Motion to approve the proposal o f Hazel Reinhardt Consulting Services to complete an Enrollment Projection Study and Housing Unit Study at a cost not to exceed $9,300.00 

3. School/Site Improvement Plans. 

Over the last several Board meetings. Board members have had an opportunity to hear presentations for each of the elementary and secondary buildings, the Area Learning Center and the Community Services Division concerning their progress on their 2012-13 school improvement plans as well as their continuous site improvement plan for the 2013-14 school year. Each site identified one or more achievement and climate goals and provided specific activities, benchmarks and evaluation criteria that will be used to chart their progress in supporting increased student achievement and enhanced building climate. The action o f the Board is to affirm the work o f each site in the development and implementation o f these plans. 

Superintendent's Recommendation: Motion to approve the seven site improvement plans submitted by building or program staffs for the 2013-14 school year. 

B. Items for Consent Grouping 

Superintendent’s Recommendation: Motion to approve the following items listed under the Consent Grouping. 

1. Region Facilities Use Agreement. 

The School Board is asked to approve the enclosed Region Facilities Use Agreement with the Minnesota State High School League (MSHSL). The MSHSL is formalizing a process that has been in place in Northfield for several years. Anyone employed for a Region 1AA game needs to be an employee of the Northfield Public Schools and not the MSHSL. 

2. Grant Application to the MN State High School League Foundation. 

Northfield High School is requesting a $5,000.00 grant from the MSHSL Foundation to be used as core funding for the RALIE and Life o f an Athlete programs. The grant application materials are enclosed. 

3. Student Activity Account —Speech. 

Activities Director Tom Graupmann is requesting Board approval to designate up to $2000 from die Speech Team’s student activity account to pay for additional coaches to work with participants. The rate of pay will be $12 - $14 per hour. The Speech Team intentionally fundraised so that more coaches could be secured. 

4. Gift Agreement. 

The Board is asked to accept a $13,248.29 gift from the Greenvale Park PTO to Greenvale Park Elementary School to be used at Greenvale Park as follows: 

Field Trip Fund for Students - $5,258.00; Licensed Staff Classroom Funds - $4,200.00; 

Funds for Specialists - $2,573.72; Music Teacher Funds - $600.00; Music Bleachers - $616.57

## STED Leadership for a ,lat World 

George J. Petersen, Ph.D. James L. Gentilucci, Ph.D. Educational Leadership and Administration Program California Polytechnic State University San Luis Obispo
